        self.subscription = self.create_subscription(
            Float32, 'distance', self.on_distance, 10)

    def on_distance(self, message):
        threshold = float(self.get_parameter('threshold_m').value)
        if not math.isfinite(message.data):
            self.get_logger().warning('No valid distance measurement')
        elif message.data < threshold:
            self.get_logger().warning(f'Close object: {message.data:.2f} m')
        else:
            self.get_logger().info(f'Distance: {message.data:.2f} m')


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = DistanceAlert()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

The receiver reads its parameter on each message, so changing the parameter will affect the next callback. The rule uses <, meaning strictly less than: 1.0 m does not trigger a 1.0 m threshold. :.2f formats a number with two decimal places for the log; it does not change the measurement. math.isfinite rejects missing or invalid numeric readings, which will matter with real sensors.

Make Python functions discoverable as ROS executables

Open the outer setup.py. Find entry_points and replace its empty console_scripts list with these entries, keeping the rest of the file:

entry_points={
    'console_scripts': [
        'distance_source = robot_workshop.distance_source:main',
        'distance_alert = robot_workshop.distance_alert:main',
    ],
},

An entry maps the executable name on the left to package.module:function on the right. There is no .py in that import path. Saving a file alone does not register a ros2 run executable. Build in the same creation terminal, before sourcing the new student overlay:

cd ~/student_ws
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop

colcon builds packages in a workspace. --packages-select selects yours; --symlink-install uses links where supported so development edits can be reflected in the installation. Rebuild after adding an executable, dependency, launch file or data file. Restart a running node after changing its Python code.

In each running terminal, source the course setup first and then:

source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash
ros2 pkg executables robot_workshop

You should see both names. local_setup.bash adds this overlay to the underlays already loaded in the terminal. Start ros2 run robot_workshop distance_source in A and ros2 run robot_workshop distance_alert in B. In C:

ros2 topic echo /distance --once
ros2 node info /distance_alert
ros2 param set /distance_alert threshold_m 0.4

Predict which alerts disappear after the threshold change, then check the output. Restore 1.0. Package, executable, node and topic names can all differ; you chose these names in four different places.

Test your receiver independently of your publisher

Stop your source with Ctrl+C, leave the receiver running, and send known inputs:

ros2 topic pub --once /distance std_msgs/msg/Float32 '{data: 0.25}'
ros2 topic pub --once /distance std_msgs/msg/Float32 '{data: 1.0}'

The quoted text is a YAML representation of the message. The shell passes it as one argument, and ROS fills the data field. The first should warn; the second should not at threshold 1.0. If publication waits for a subscriber, check the receiver’s topic and type. This test separates a receiver defect from a source defect.

Change your publisher to send three values in a repeating sequence, including one exactly at the threshold. Decide the expected log for each before running. Then rename its output using --ros-args -r distance:=distance_test and repair your receiver connection using the same remapping. The completed package must run without importing arc_lab1. Keep its source and your three-case evidence.

The ROS command guide explains namespaces, parameter files and the build cycle for later use. The official package tutorial and publisher/subscriber tutorial show the same underlying ROS mechanisms in another application.

10. Finish this first system

Keep your student package, its build/run commands, and the three-case receiver test. Also retain one message example from the supplied system, its node names, the topic/type they share, a close-range warning and your mismatch/repair evidence. Explain what caused the warning by pointing to the source value and receiver condition. Stop both programs with Ctrl+C and follow the cleanup routine in Start here.

You now know enough ROS 2 to begin working with the robot: components exchange typed messages, and we can inspect those connections while they run. Lab 2 introduces the robot model and the coordinate frames that give its data a physical meaning.

Optional extension: use ros2 param set /range_source rate_hz 5.0 and compare the monitor’s rate. Read on_parameters() to find where the timer is rebuilt. Then try 0.0 and inspect the rejection. Restore 10.0 before finishing. Detailed delivery settings appear with sensors in Lab 3; managed startup appears with navigation servers in Lab 6.

References for this lab

  • ROS 2 beginner tutorials: use the nodes/topics tutorials to revisit the commands you ran.
  • ROS 2 communication interfaces: today’s stream is a topic; services and actions will become useful later.
  • Gazebo’s ROS 2 integration overview: preview how simulated data reaches ROS programs before Lab 3.

Lab 2: Meet the robot: its parts, coordinates and motion

In Lab 1, two nodes exchanged a distance value. Before that value can describe a real obstacle, the software needs to know where the sensor is mounted and which direction it points. Today we give our messages a robot to belong to.

Your result: a visible robot model, an explanation of its body/sensor frames, and a prediction of how its two wheels make it turn. Spend 15 minutes inspecting the reference model, 40 building your own, 25 on frames and wheel calculations, 25 testing a change and 15 saving results. Use Start here to prepare two terminals. Stop any previous lab programs first.

Before you open the robot description

A robot model is a set of data describing parts and how they connect. It is not a photograph, and it does not decide how to move. Picture a small cart: the body is one rigid part, each wheel is another, and the laser is another. In URDF, these parts are links. The connections are joints. A fixed joint attaches the laser firmly to the body; a rotating joint lets a wheel turn.

A coordinate is a number that locates something relative to a chosen origin and direction. A coordinate frame supplies that origin and those directions. If the sensor is 0.10 m ahead of the body origin, a wall 1.00 m ahead of the sensor is 1.10 m ahead of the body origin when both frames point the same way. Both measurements describe the same wall. Their reference points differ.

The files use XML, a format with opening and closing tags. URDF is the vocabulary describing the robot. Xacro adds reusable values before producing the URDF. Read the illustrated file examples in the ROS guide if these names are new. Today you will connect each piece of text to the shape or relationship it creates.

1. Open the robot model

In terminal A:

ros2 launch arc_description display.launch.py

In Lab 1, ros2 run started one executable. Here ros2 launch reads a launch file, which describes a group of programs and their settings. The package is arc_description and the launch filename is display.launch.py.

You should see RViz and a small joint-state control window. RViz displays our robot: a body, two drive wheels, a support wheel and a laser sensor. Use the mouse to inspect it from different angles. Moving a wheel slider changes the displayed joint position. The robot will not drive across a floor: this launch shows geometry and joints, with no Gazebo physics running.

Open arc_description/launch/display.launch.py and find its Node(...) entries. robot_state_publisher works out where robot parts are from the model and joint positions. joint_state_publisher_gui supplies positions from the sliders. rviz2 displays the result. You can inspect them with the same ros2 node list command you used in Lab 1.

2. Find a body part and the connection that holds it

Open arc_description/urdf/arc_bot.urdf.xacro in your editor. This is the course robot description. Read .urdf.xacro as “a robot description that uses Xacro.” Xacro expands its reusable values and expressions into a URDF description, written in XML. We will identify one part and one connection before editing anything.

Find <link name="base_link">. A link represents a rigid part. Find a <joint ...> with a parent and child: a joint connects two links and defines their relative position and permitted motion. A fixed sensor mount does not rotate; a wheel joint does.

The body has three descriptions serving different purposes:

Description Meaning What would a mistake affect?
visual The shape drawn on screen What you see
collision The shape tested for contact Whether the simulated body hits another object
inertial Mass and resistance to changes in motion How physics responds to forces

Keep that distinction in mind for Lab 3. A good-looking robot is not enough to prove that the simulator has the correct collision shape or dynamics.

3. Give “in front of the robot” a precise meaning

A coordinate frame is an origin plus named directions from which positions are measured. Think of attaching a small set of x/y/z axes to each part. In our robot convention, x points forward, y left and z upward. Distances are in metres.

base_link is attached to the body. laser_link is attached to the laser. The laser is mounted 0.10 m ahead of the body origin. Suppose it measures a wall 1.00 m directly ahead. With this aligned mounting, the wall is 1.10 m ahead of the body origin. Reporting 1.00 m without saying which origin it uses leaves an ambiguity that a map cannot resolve.

A transform describes how one frame is positioned and rotated relative to another. tf2 is the ROS 2 system that stores and looks up these relationships. The connected relationships form a frame tree.

In terminal B:

ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link laser_link

This runs a supplied transform-inspection program. Look for a translation whose x value is approximately 0.10 m. There is also a vertical offset. Stop the repeating output with Ctrl+C. You have checked the sensor mounting from the running system rather than just reading a picture.

ros2 topic echo /joint_states --once

This is another typed message, just as /range was. It contains named joints and their positions. Move a slider and inspect a new message. The model plus these positions tells robot_state_publisher where the moving wheel links are.

The frame base_footprint is a ground-level reference below the body. Later, odom will provide a reference for the robot’s accumulated local movement. This display-only launch does not need the odom frame, because the base is not being driven through a simulated world yet.

Build a small robot description and launch it yourself

The supplied model has enough detail for physics. Begin your own description with two rigid pieces: a rectangular body and a sensor attached above it. Continue the robot_workshop package from Lab 1. Create urdf and launch directories beside its setup.py:

mkdir -p ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/urdf
mkdir -p ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/launch

Write urdf/student_robot.urdf:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<robot name="student_robot">
  <link name="base_link">
    <visual>
      <geometry><box size="0.40 0.30 0.15"/></geometry>
      <material name="body_blue"><color rgba="0.1 0.4 0.8 1"/></material>
    </visual>
  </link>
  <link name="sensor_link">
    <visual>
      <geometry><cylinder radius="0.03" length="0.04"/></geometry>
    </visual>
  </link>
  <joint name="sensor_mount" type="fixed">
    <parent link="base_link"/>
    <child link="sensor_link"/>
    <origin xyz="0.10 0 0.12" rpy="0 0 0"/>
  </joint>
</robot>

XML uses opening and closing tags to group information. size="0.40 0.30 0.15" gives the box lengths along x, y and z, in metres. xyz locates the child joint origin in its parent frame; rpy is roll, pitch and yaw in radians. All three rotations are zero here. rgba gives red, green, blue and opacity on a 0 to 1 scale. This first model defines visuals and a fixed joint only. Adding physics would require collision shapes and appropriate mass/inertia values.

Now write launch/model.launch.py:

from pathlib import Path
from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch_ros.actions import Node


def generate_launch_description():
    share = Path(get_package_share_directory('robot_workshop'))
    description = (share / 'urdf' / 'student_robot.urdf').read_text()
    return LaunchDescription([
        Node(package='robot_state_publisher', executable='robot_state_publisher',
             parameters=[{'robot_description': description}], output='screen'),
        Node(package='rviz2', executable='rviz2',
             arguments=['-f', 'base_link'], output='screen'),
    ])

The launch function returns the processes to start. get_package_share_directory finds installed package data, avoiding a path tied to your username. read_text() loads the URDF as a Python string. robot_description receives that string; robot_state_publisher publishes the fixed relationship. There are no moving joints in this small model, so it needs no joint-state slider node.

In setup.py, add from glob import glob at the top. Add these two tuples inside the existing data_files list, preserving the package/resource entries:

('share/' + package_name + '/launch', glob('launch/*.launch.py')),
('share/' + package_name + '/urdf', glob('urdf/*.urdf')),

glob finds matching files. Each tuple says where those files are installed. Without these entries, the source files may exist but ros2 launch cannot find them in the installed package. Add the following dependency lines inside package.xml, before <export>:

<exec_depend>launch</exec_depend>
<exec_depend>launch_ros</exec_depend>
<exec_depend>ament_index_python</exec_depend>
<exec_depend>robot_state_publisher</exec_depend>
<exec_depend>rviz2</exec_depend>

Use the Lab 1 build command in a fresh terminal with the course underlay, then source the student overlay in a running terminal. Stop the supplied model launch first so two publishers do not claim the same body frame.

ros2 launch robot_workshop model.launch.py

In RViz, click Add, choose RobotModel, and set its Description Topic to /robot_description if needed. The Fixed Frame should be base_link. In another prepared terminal:

ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link sensor_link

Check the x and z translations against your XML. Change the sensor’s x mount to 0.20 m, rebuild and relaunch, and predict the new translation before checking. Return it to 0.10 m. You have now authored geometry, installed package data and composed two standard ROS programs in your own launch file.

For your next project, use ros2 launch PACKAGE FILE --show-args to discover a launch file’s declared options. A launch argument configures the launch; a node parameter configures a node. They are connected only when the launch file explicitly passes one into the other. See the launch integration tutorial.

Read the wheel equations one quantity at a time

A radius is the distance from a circle’s centre to its edge. Rotating through one radian moves a point on the rim through an arc equal to the radius. This is why rim speed = radius × angular speed: 0.05 m times 4 rad/s gives 0.20 m/s. Radians measure angle; pi radians is half a turn, or 180 degrees.

For the next equations, omega_L and omega_R are wheel angular speeds, v is body forward speed, omega is body turning speed, and L is the left-to-right wheel separation. Subscripts label quantities; they do not mean multiplication. Average the two rim speeds to get forward speed. Subtract the left speed from the right and divide by separation to get turn rate. These relations assume rolling without sideways slip on a flat surface.

If the rims move at 0.10 and 0.30 m/s, their average is 0.20 m/s. Their difference is 0.20 m/s, so the turn rate is 0.20 / 0.35, about 0.571 rad/s. Swapping left and right changes the turn’s sign while leaving the average unchanged. This is the physical reasoning behind the formulas below.

4. Make a prediction before driving

Our robot uses differential drive: left and right wheels are commanded independently. If both rims move forward at the same speed, the robot goes straight. If the right rim moves faster, the robot turns left. Equal and opposite rim speeds turn it about its axle centre.

A controller expresses the intended body motion as two quantities:

  • v: forward speed in metres per second.
  • omega: turning speed in radians per second. Positive means a left turn when viewed from above. One complete revolution is 2*pi radians.

Wheel speed is also an angular speed. Multiplying a wheel’s angular speed by its radius gives its rim speed. For wheel radius r = 0.050 m and separation L = 0.350 m, the average rim speed produces translation and the difference produces rotation:

[ v=(_R+_L), =(_R-_L). ]

To solve the reverse problem, split the turning contribution equally across the wheels: the left rim needs v - omega*L/2 and the right rim needs v + omega*L/2. Divide each by radius to get wheel angular speeds. For v=0.20, omega=0.50 and L=0.35, the turning contribution is 0.0875 m/s. The rims therefore need 0.1125 and 0.2875 m/s, which become 2.25 and 5.75 rad/s at radius 0.05 m. This calculation explains the second printed case below.

For a straight drive at 0.20 m/s, both wheels need 0.20 / 0.05 = 4 rad/s. The equations are useful because they translate between a robot-level request and the individual wheel commands needed to realise it.

Run this small example from the repository root. Copy the whole block, including the final PY; it runs a short Python script without creating a new file:

python3 - <<'PY'
from starters.lab02.diffdrive import inverse_kinematics, forward_kinematics
for v, turn in [(0.20, 0.0), (0.20, 0.50), (0.0, 0.50)]:
    left, right = inverse_kinematics(v, turn)
    print('body request:', v, turn)
    print('wheel rad/s:', left, right)
    print('recovered body motion:', forward_kinematics(left, right))
PY

The straight case gives about 4 and 4 rad/s. The forward-left case gives about 2.25 and 5.75 rad/s. The turning-in-place case gives about -1.75 and 1.75 rad/s. Match each pair to your predicted motion. inverse_kinematics() converts body motion to wheel motion; forward_kinematics() checks the reverse calculation. These function names describe opposite directions of the same relationship.

Read the left panel first: with constant forward speed, increasing turn speed makes a tighter arc. For the 0.20 m/s, 0.50 rad/s case the turning radius is v/omega = 0.40 m. In Lab 3 you will watch a simulated robot move and compare its direction with this prediction.

5. Repair a display that has lost its reference

In RViz, find Global Options → Fixed Frame. This setting chooses the frame from which the viewer displays everything. Note its working value first. Change it to missing_frame, a name our robot does not publish.

RViz should report a frame/transform problem. The source programs have not changed; the viewer is asking for a relationship the system cannot supply. Restore the original working frame, or choose base_link, and check that the robot is visible again. Explain the repair using “origin and directions,” rather than treating a frame name as an arbitrary setting to try.

For a complete frame report, run:

ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames

Open the report file named in the output. Locate the body, laser and wheel branches. This will be a useful reference when you inspect scan frames in Lab 3.

Finish and carry the model into simulation

Save the frame report, the measured laser offset and your three wheel-speed predictions. Explain why turning a slider changes a joint but does not drive the base. Stop the launch with Ctrl+C and use the cleanup routine in Start here. The core lab is complete. Next, Gazebo will add a world, physics and sensor measurements to this description.

Optional investigation: calibration: the plot’s right panel assumes a physical wheel radius of 0.050 m but an odometry calculation using 0.055 m. Odometry estimates movement from motion feedback, such as wheel rotation. For the same measured rotation this radius error reports 10% too much travel. Use odometry_scale_error() in starters/lab02/diffdrive.py to check the ratio. Propose an independent distance measurement to verify it; do not use an estimate derived from those same wheel measurements as your ground truth.

If the display launch fails: a robot_description YAML-parsing error means the generated XML has not been explicitly treated as a string. The supplied fixed launch uses ParameterValue(..., value_type=str). Install the corrected arc_description/launch/display.launch.py, rebuild arc_description and source the workspace using Start here. This is troubleshooting guidance, not a required fault to introduce into your working model.

References for this lab

  • ROS 2 tf2 overview: revisit frame relationships after inspecting the robot.
  • Modern Robotics book resources: Chapters 2-3 develop coordinates; Chapter 13 develops wheeled motion.
  • Jazzy differential-drive controller: the controller that will implement the wheel/body relationship in simulation.

Lab 3: Collect a sensor run that can be trusted

In Lab 1 you inspected a stream of numbers. In Lab 2 you gave the robot named parts and coordinate frames. Today Gazebo puts that robot in a room: you will drive it, watch what its laser sees and save the messages for the next lab.

Two-hour mission: drive a short warehouse inspection and save the data needed to map it. Before recording, prove that the scan’s values, frame and timestamps are meaningful. The output is an MCAP bag used directly in Lab 4.

Plan 15 minutes for simulation startup, 35 for your sensor node, 20 for timing and a frame fault, 35 for recording/replay and 15 for your result. Follow the shared terminal setup. Close the Lab 2 display launch: the simulator starts its own robot-state publisher.

What changes when the distance comes from a sensor?

In Lab 1 we invented one distance at a time. A laser scanner measures distances in many directions. One scan is a set of readings, with information about the directions and when the measurement was made. A beam is one of those directions. A simulated scan represents what the simulated sensor sees in Gazebo’s world.

Three questions now matter: which direction does each number describe, is the number a valid measurement, and when was it measured? A timestamp records a time. A frame ID names the coordinate frame in which the measurement is described. QoS means the ROS delivery settings. A bag is a recording of ROS messages for later inspection or replay. We will inspect these properties before trusting the data in a map.

Start the physical simulation and see its data

The robot’s laser scanner, or lidar, measures distances in many directions. One scan is the collection of those measurements for one sweep. Gazebo calculates the readings from the simulated objects. We will display them in RViz, just as we displayed the robot model last week.

Terminal A:

ros2 launch arc_gazebo simulation.launch.py headless:=true

Terminal B:

rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix --share arc_gazebo)/rviz/simulation.rviz" \
  --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

Wait for the controllers to activate. RViz should show the robot and a scan corresponding to nearby warehouse surfaces. headless:=true removes the Gazebo GUI; it does not remove the rendering needed by the GPU lidar. If graphics fail, run course-check in the VM and resolve the reported graphics issue before interpreting the scan as a sensing algorithm failure.

Read arc_gazebo/config/ros_gz_bridge.yaml. The bridge converts selected Gazebo Transport messages to ROS messages. Here /scan, /imu and /clock cross that boundary. Wheel commands and odometry use the Gazebo ros2_control integration; they are not all routed through the same sensor bridge. This explains why a working /odom topic does not prove that the laser bridge is configured.

Check a scan as a measurement

The new topic is /scan. Start with the same tools you already know. In terminal C, inspect its connections and one message:

ros2 topic info /scan --verbose
ros2 topic echo /scan --once --qos-reliability best_effort

The extra --qos-reliability best_effort selects a delivery setting suitable for this sensor. Quality of Service (QoS) describes how messages should be delivered and retained. Best effort allows lost samples; reliable delivery can retry them. A subscriber requiring reliable delivery cannot receive from a publisher offering only best effort. The verbose topic information shows these settings. Today, use the supplied compatible setting and first confirm data arrives; comparing all QoS policies is not needed to complete the recording.

The message has a ranges array rather than one data field. Its header identifies the measurement time and coordinate frame. Its angle fields tell us which direction belongs to each range. Now inspect the robot’s motion estimate:

ros2 topic echo /odom --once

Odometry is an estimate of movement built from wheel feedback in this robot. The message includes position, orientation and velocity. A controller turns the requested body velocity into wheel commands. These commands inspect that controller and the transform needed to place the laser readings:

ros2 control list_controllers
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo odom laser_link

Stop the transform echo when you have seen several updates. The laser has 360 beams across a full revolution and configured range bounds 0.12-12 m. Check those fields in the actual message. Beam i has bearing angle_min + i * angle_increment in header.frame_id, at the measurement’s timestamp. Its endpoint cannot be placed on a map by using the range alone.

Look at the values while stationary and after a small turn. A correct count and rate can coexist with a broken sensor. If nearly every beam stays at the minimum range, inspect sensor rendering and whether the sensor’s own visual housing blocks its rays. If walls move with the robot in RViz, inspect the frame/time chain before adjusting noise parameters.

To move manually, start this in a separate terminal and keep keyboard focus in it:

ros2 run teleop_twist_keyboard teleop_twist_keyboard

Use the help printed by the program: i drives forward, j and l turn, k stops, and z reduces speed. Begin slowly, stop before inspecting another window, and close teleoperation before starting an autonomous command source. Watch /odom and the scan while making the forward-left turn predicted in Lab 2. Wheel odometry may start at its own origin even though Gazebo spawns the robot at world coordinates (1,1); these are different frames.

Build a sensor-processing node and reuse your first receiver

A useful ROS component transforms an input into an output with a clear meaning. Your task is to turn /scan into one distance for the 30-degree sector centred on the robot’s forward axis. The output will use the same Float32 interface as your Lab 1 pretend sensor. Stop distance_source; only one producer should supply that stream during this comparison.

First discover the structure rather than guessing its array order:

ros2 topic type /scan
ros2 interface show sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan
ros2 topic hz /scan

Stop hz with Ctrl+C after a sample window. Array indices start at zero. If angle_min=-pi, the first ray points backwards, not forwards. For index i, add i * angle_increment to angle_min. For example, with a one-degree increment, index 180 would point forward from a -180-degree start. Use the actual increment; 360 samples do not guarantee exactly one degree between them.

The header stamp refers to the first ray. time_increment, when populated, describes the interval between rays. Treating an entire scan as simultaneous is an approximation that becomes less accurate as motion during a scan increases. These meanings come from the LaserScan definition.

Write the filter in plain language first: compute each ray’s angle; keep rays within 15 degrees of forward; reject invalid or out-of-range distances; take the smallest remaining value. Now implement front_range.py:

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from std_msgs.msg import Float32


def front_min(ranges, angle_min, angle_increment, range_min, range_max):
    valid = []
    for index, distance in enumerate(ranges):
        angle = angle_min + index * angle_increment
        angle = math.atan2(math.sin(angle), math.cos(angle))
        if abs(angle) <= math.radians(15):
            if math.isfinite(distance) and range_min <= distance <= range_max:
                valid.append(distance)
    return min(valid) if valid else float('nan')


class FrontRange(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('front_range')
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Float32, 'distance', 10)
        self.subscription = self.create_subscription(
            LaserScan, '/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)

    def on_scan(self, scan):
        message = Float32()
        message.data = float(front_min(scan.ranges, scan.angle_min,
                                      scan.angle_increment, scan.range_min,
                                      scan.range_max))
        self.publisher.publish(message)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = FrontRange()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

The enumerate loop supplies an index and value together. abs(angle) measures angle magnitude, so the same bound covers left and right. radians(15) converts degrees to the radians used by the message. atan2(sin(angle), cos(angle)) wraps equivalent angles into a signed turn between -pi and pi. This also works if a driver reports angles from 0 to 2*pi.

No valid ray produces NaN, a numeric marker for unavailable data. Your receiver already reports it as invalid. This deliberately conservative rule also rejects infinite no-return rays; a production implementation needs driver-specific validity handling. The front-sector minimum is distance from the sensor to a surface. It is not the robot body’s clearance or a collision guarantee.

Save the file as ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/front_range.py. Add 'front_range = robot_workshop.front_range:main', inside the existing console_scripts list in your package’s setup.py. Keep the earlier entries. Add <exec_depend>sensor_msgs</exec_depend> to package.xml. Build in a fresh terminal with the course underlay sourced, as in Lab 1:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/arc_ws/install/setup.bash
cd ~/student_ws
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop

In every terminal that will run your program, use source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup.

With the healthy simulator running, start these in separate prepared terminals:

ros2 run robot_workshop front_range --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true
ros2 run robot_workshop distance_alert

Use ros2 topic echo /distance --once and compare it with the visible front sector in RViz. Turn slowly toward a wall; do not drive into it to test a log. The receiver now works with a simulated sensor without knowing Gazebo exists. Change the filter’s sector from 15 to 30 degrees on either side and explain which extra obstacles may influence the minimum. Save both your prediction and the measured difference, then restore the intended sector.

For portability, remapping can replace the absolute input with another sensor: --ros-args -r /scan:=/other_scan. For a new project, you would first discover that topic’s type, angular coverage, frame and QoS, then verify compatibility. A matching name alone is insufficient.

Separate sensor time from computer time

The real computer has a clock, and the simulation has a clock. A busy VM can take longer than one real second to calculate one second of simulated motion. ROS nodes using use_sim_time:=true use the simulation’s /clock topic, keeping their times consistent with the simulated measurements. This parameter does not make the simulator run faster; it selects the time reference.

ros2 run arc_lab3 sensor_doctor --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

The doctor gathers 100 scans, computes intervals from message header timestamps, and compares those stamps with its ROS clock. At 10 Hz simulation time it needs about ten simulated seconds per report. If the VM runs slower than real time, the wall-clock wait will be longer.

Run ros2 topic hz /scan in another terminal for a separate receive-rate check. A real-time factor of 0.8 can yield roughly 8 arrivals per wall second from a sensor configured at 10 Hz simulation time. The header intervals distinguish that case from a sensor actually configured to sample at 8 Hz. Neither measure alone describes the whole pipeline.

Optional clock fault: stop the doctor and restart it once with -p use_sim_time:=false. A very large stamp difference is expected when wall-epoch time is compared with simulation time. That difference is not a measured network delay. Restore true before recording evidence. When timestamps and receive time share a clock, their difference becomes a useful diagnostic, though scheduling and transport both contribute to it.

Isolate one fault, then restore the baseline

Stop the running programs and use arc-clean. Start one deliberately faulty world in terminal A:

ros2 launch arc_gazebo simulation.launch.py world:=broken_b headless:=true

Repeat the scan echo, sensor doctor and TF inspection. The scan should still arrive, but its frame is laser_link_v2, which is absent from the robot model. That is a mismatch between the message’s declared coordinate frame and the TF tree. Changing RViz’s fixed frame cannot create the missing transform.

Locate the fault == 'b' selection in arc_description/urdf/arc_bot.gazebo.xacro. The repair is to make the declared frame agree with the real sensor frame, not to rename arbitrary unrelated frames until the warning disappears. Restore the healthy launch by stopping everything, running arc-clean and launching without world:=broken_b. Confirm that /scan now declares laser_link and can be transformed to odom.

If time allows, investigate one additional fault. broken_a reduces scan rate to 3 Hz; broken_c increases range noise standard deviation to 1.0 m. Record the observable that distinguishes each from a missing TF frame. Do not debug several injected faults simultaneously.

Record a route with enough information to reconstruct it

An MCAP bag is a recording of messages over time. Saving a bag lets you repeat an analysis on the same journey instead of driving a different route each time. It is not a video: it preserves the robot data that our mapper needs.

Start a fresh healthy simulation. In a recording terminal:

mkdir -p "$HOME/arc_ws/bags"
ros2 bag record --storage mcap -o "$HOME/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run" \
  /scan /odom /tf /tf_static /clock /joint_states

The output directory must be new; use _v2 for another run. Drive slowly around one connected area for two or three minutes, facing surfaces from several directions. A short route with turns and revisited walls is more useful than spinning once. Keep the recorder running throughout the motion, then stop it with Ctrl+C so it can finish writing metadata.

ros2 bag info "$HOME/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run"

Check that /scan and /odom both contain many messages. The bag includes sensor data, relative robot motion and the transforms needed to interpret the data. It is an experimental record you can process repeatedly without changing the physical route every time you edit a mapping algorithm.

Replay without competing clocks

Stop the simulator, teleoperation and other live publishers. Run arc-clean. Play only the selected recorded data topics and let the player generate /clock:

ros2 bag play "$HOME/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run" --clock \
  --topics /scan /odom /tf /tf_static /joint_states

The original bag also contains /clock, but this topic filter excludes it. Playing recorded /clock while also generating a playback clock would create two clock streams. Start the doctor with use_sim_time:=true before playback if you want to inspect the entire run; start RViz with the same setting to watch the recorded motion.

Keep the bag path, healthy frame/rate evidence, a scan screenshot and the fault/repair explanation. Lab 4 will use the recorded headers and odometry to place each beam in a grid. Stop playback before leaving the session.

References for this lab

  • Gazebo Harmonic and ROS 2 integration: inspect which conversions the bridge actually supports.
  • ROS 2 time design: explains clock domains, simulation and time jumps behind the doctor’s report.
  • ROS 2 QoS settings: return to delivery compatibility if a discovered sensor topic produces no received data.
  • Foxglove: MCAP as the ROS 2 default bag format: an industry explanation of the recording format used for your repeatable experiment.

Lab 4: Turn the recorded journey into a map

You now have a recording of what the laser measured and where the robot thought it was. Today we combine those two messages. A distance reading becomes a line on a floor plan, and repeated lines gradually reveal the room.

Two-hour mission: build an occupancy map from the Lab 3 bag, locate a geometric defect, and explain how repeated observations change a cell’s state. Your map will also show why estimating motion and constructing a map cannot always be treated as independent problems.

Budget 15 minutes for the bag, 25 for the mapper and geometry, 35 for your map publisher, 30 for the shifted-wall comparison and 15 for your result. Use the shared setup in the ROS VM. No live simulator is needed. Have ~/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run available; a classmate’s clearly attributed bag is acceptable if your recording did not finish.

What do we mean by making a map?

Imagine covering the floor with square tiles and storing one number for each tile. This is a grid map. A cell is one square. We want to distinguish space the sensor observed as empty, space where it detected an obstacle, and space it has not observed. Unknown does not mean empty.

A laser reading gives a distance and direction from the sensor. To place it in the map, we also need the sensor’s position and orientation when the reading was taken. The calculation below turns that local measurement into a map location. Resolution tells us the side length of one cell in metres. With 0.1 m cells, ten cells span one metre. Probability represents uncertainty about occupancy; it is not the physical fraction of a cell painted by an obstacle.

Reconstruct what the sensor saw

An occupancy grid is a floor plan divided into square cells. At 0.05 m resolution, each cell represents a 5 cm by 5 cm patch of floor. Resolution means metres per cell; the origin says where the grid starts in the chosen coordinate frame. Without those two values, a picture cannot tell the robot where an obstacle is in metres.

The map is a two-dimensional array of beliefs about space. A cell is not “free” because the robot has not hit it. It becomes more likely free when a valid beam passes through it, and more likely occupied when a valid obstacle return ends there. Unobserved space stays unknown.

Read teaching/map_bag.py with starters/lab04/occupancy.py open beside it. The helper supplies data handling; the starter implements the actual map update.

For each selected scan, the helper finds the nearest odometry header stamp. It rejects matches more than 0.10 s away and reports the largest accepted gap. Using message receipt order alone would confuse communication delay with the time the measurement was taken. Nearest-neighbour matching is deliberately simple: interpolation can improve it, and fast motion would also require thinking about motion during the scan itself.

The odometry gives the base pose (x, y, theta). The sensor sits 0.10 m ahead, so its planar position is:

[ x_s=x+0.10,y_s=y+0.10. ]

For range r at local bearing a, the endpoint is (x_s + r*cos(theta+a), y_s + r*sin(theta+a)). Using the base position directly moves each measured obstacle to the wrong place. During rotation the error changes direction, which can turn a thin wall into a thick or doubled wall.

Work one endpoint out by hand

On a top-down drawing, theta is the robot’s heading from the positive x axis; a is a ray’s direction relative to the sensor. Cosine gives the fraction of a unit arrow along x, and sine gives its fraction along y. For angles 0, 90 and 180 degrees the direction pairs are (1,0), (0,1) and (-1,0). Multiplying that pair by distance gives the x/y displacement of the ray.

Suppose the base is at (1,2) m, faces along positive y (theta=pi/2), and measures a wall 2 m straight ahead (a=0). The forward sensor mount moves its origin to (1,2.1). The endpoint becomes (1,4.1) m. Omitting the mount would place it at (1,4.0). Draw the base, sensor and endpoint as three distinct marks.

To locate a grid cell, subtract the grid origin and divide by metres per cell. Then take the mathematical floor, which rounds down. With origin x=-2 m and resolution 0.05 m, x=1 m gives column (1-(-2))/0.05 = 60. A point just below an origin belongs outside the grid; converting -0.2 to an integer would give zero in Python, so int() is not a general substitute for floor. Always check bounds before indexing an array.

Make the first complete map

python3 -m teaching.map_bag \
  --bag "$HOME/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run" \
  --out results/lab04_reference
xdg-open results/lab04_reference/map.png

The helper writes map.pgm, map.yaml, map.png, log_odds.npy and report.json. The PNG is for inspection. The PGM/YAML pair carries image, resolution and origin for a map server. The NumPy array preserves the accumulated evidence before thresholding, and the report records scan count, timing gaps, coverage and sensor offset. A displayed map alone cannot tell you whether most input scans were silently skipped.

The supplied grid covers x and y from -2 to 12 m in the odometry frame, at 0.05 m resolution. This is a practical bound for a short course run, not an automatic choice for every warehouse. A route outside the grid needs a larger grid or a different origin. The helper skips out-of-bounds sensor poses and records skipped scans. It processes every third scan by default to keep the first run manageable; --stride 1 uses all scans.

Check the output before modifying the algorithm: are walls recognisable, does the free area follow the recorded route, and are unknown areas left grey? If there is no usable map, inspect the report and the bag’s /scan and /odom headers before changing occupancy thresholds.

Understand one cell before changing the whole grid

Consider three cells in a row between the sensor and a wall. If the beam travels through the first two and hits the third, it supports “free” for the first two and “occupied” for the third. A cell outside the beam receives no evidence. Because sensing and pose estimates have errors, we accumulate confidence rather than permanently deciding from a single reading. Probability near 0 means likely free, near 1 means likely occupied, and 0.5 represents our initial lack of preference between the two.

Odds compare the chance of occupancy with the chance of being free. For probability p=0.8, the odds are 0.8/0.2=4: four to one in favour of occupancy. Taking the natural logarithm converts multiplication of odds into addition, which makes repeated evidence updates inexpensive. log(1)=0, so equal odds start at zero. e is the base of the natural logarithm, about 2.718; exp(x) calculates e raised to the power x.

In the formula below, l_old is the stored evidence before an observation, Delta l is this observation’s increment, and clip restricts the result to a chosen interval. Two hits from zero give l=1.70 and probability about 0.846. One later free observation changes this to l=1.30, or about 0.786. Evidence can therefore support occupancy without making a cell permanently occupied.

The reference stores log odds l = log(p/(1-p)). Probability 0.5 corresponds to zero log odds, a useful initial value for unknown space. Under the simplified independent-observation model, a hit adds 0.85 and free-space evidence adds -0.40:

[ l_{new}=(l_{old}+l,-5,5), p=. ]

These increments are sensor-model choices. They do not mean a lidar return is correct with probability 0.85. One hit from the prior gives approximately 0.701 occupancy probability; one free observation gives approximately 0.401.

python3 - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from starters.lab04.occupancy import OccupancyMap
m = OccupancyMap(4, 4)
m.integrate_scan((1.0, 1.0, 0.0), np.array([1.0]), np.array([0.0]))
for label, point in [('ray interior', (1.5, 1.0)), ('hit', (2.0, 1.0))]:
    row, col = m.world_to_cell(*point)
    print(label, float(m.log_odds[row, col]), float(m.probability()[row, col]))
PY

Trace the call into bresenham(): it enumerates grid cells along a ray. The interior cells receive free evidence and the endpoint receives hit evidence. Clamping limits confidence so that later contradictory observations can revise a cell. It also prevents repeated correlated scans from accumulating unlimited certainty, though clamping alone does not make the independence assumption true.

The exported trinary map uses 100 for occupied probability at least 0.65, 0 for free probability at most 0.25, and -1 for the uncertain interval. This means one free observation does not immediately label a cell free. The PGM representation uses different pixel values and vertically flips the array for image storage; read the YAML as well as the picture when interpreting coordinates.

Publish a map you constructed yourself

Before a whole-room mapper, build the smallest useful mapping result: one horizontal laser ray in a small grid. Use unknown for unobserved cells, free for cells crossed by the ray, and occupied for its endpoint. This exposes both the algorithm and the ROS map interface without hiding either inside a helper.

An OccupancyGrid stores its cells as one flat list in row-major order. In a 20-column grid, row 4 begins at index 4*20=80; column 8 is index 88. The ROS message allows application-dependent occupancy values. Our classroom map and the Nav2 map workflow use -1 for unknown, 0 for free and 100 for occupied. The shape is 10 rows by 20 columns, so the data list must contain 200 entries.

Write small_map.py. Begin with horizontal_ray() and verify its indices on paper before writing the ROS node:

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from nav_msgs.msg import OccupancyGrid
from rclpy.qos import QoSProfile, DurabilityPolicy, ReliabilityPolicy


def horizontal_ray(width, height, row, start_col, hit_col):
    if not (0 <= row < height and 0 <= start_col < hit_col < width):
        raise ValueError('The horizontal ray must fit inside the grid')
    data = [-1] * (width * height)
    for col in range(start_col, hit_col):
        data[row * width + col] = 0
    data[row * width + hit_col] = 100
    return data


class SmallMap(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('small_map')
        qos = QoSProfile(depth=1, reliability=ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE,
                         durability=DurabilityPolicy.TRANSIENT_LOCAL)
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(OccupancyGrid, 'student_map', qos)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_map)

    def publish_map(self):
        message = OccupancyGrid()
        message.header.frame_id = 'odom'
        message.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        message.info.resolution = 0.1
        message.info.width = 20
        message.info.height = 10
        message.info.origin.orientation.w = 1.0
        message.data = horizontal_ray(20, 10, row=4, start_col=2, hit_col=8)
        self.publisher.publish(message)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = SmallMap()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

[-1] * 200 creates 200 unknown entries. range(start_col, hit_col) excludes the final column, which lets us treat the hit separately. The map covers 2 m by 1 m at 0.1 m per cell. The identity orientation has quaternion w=1, with x, y and z zero; an all-zero quaternion does not describe a valid rotation.

The publisher uses reliable, transient-local delivery and retains one sample. A compatible late-joining subscriber can receive the retained map while the publisher exists. Sensor streams usually favour recent samples; maps often need this retained state. The node also republishes once a second so you can watch its header change. QoS does not turn the topic into a permanent disk file.

Save the file as ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/small_map.py. Add 'small_map = robot_workshop.small_map:main', inside the existing console_scripts list in your package’s setup.py. Keep the earlier entries. Add <exec_depend>nav_msgs</exec_depend> to package.xml. Build in a fresh terminal with the course underlay sourced, as in Lab 1:

source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source ~/arc_ws/install/setup.bash
cd ~/student_ws
colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop

In every terminal that will run your program, use source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup.

No simulator is needed for this small static map. Run your node in one terminal:

ros2 run robot_workshop small_map

In another:

ros2 topic info /student_map --verbose
ros2 topic echo /student_map --once --qos-durability transient_local
rviz2 -f odom

In RViz add a Map display, select /student_map, and choose Transient Local durability if needed. You should see one free row segment, one occupied endpoint and unknown elsewhere. Since the map and viewer use odom, this static example does not need a transform to another frame.

Change the hit column from 8 to 12. Predict a 0.4 m shift of the occupied cell, then restart and verify it. Finally extend your function to handle a ray pointing left, keeping its endpoint occupied. Decide how the iteration direction changes; reversing the meaning of free and occupied is not the repair.

The full bag mapper adds arbitrary ray angles, time-matched poses and accumulated uncertainty to this same input-to-cell idea. Your small node produces a standard ROS map message, so a ROS viewer can display it without a course-specific reader. Stop the node and RViz before returning to the saved bag comparison.

Solve a shifted-wall problem with a controlled experiment

Build a second map from the same bag, deliberately pretending the sensor is at the base origin:

python3 -m teaching.map_bag \
  --bag "$HOME/arc_ws/bags/lab03_mapping_run" \
  --laser-x 0.0 --out results/lab04_wrong_offset
xdg-open results/lab04_wrong_offset/map.png

Use the same resolution and stride. Compare a wall seen before and after a turn, rather than comparing unrelated parts of the two images. Explain the change using the rotating offset vector. If the short route does not make the effect visible, report that limitation and choose a section with different headings; do not invent an improvement.

Restore --laser-x 0.10, then choose one further change based on an observed defect. For example, use --stride 1 if coverage is sparse, or compare resolution 0.05 with 0.10 m if wall roughness is dominated by pose/measurement uncertainty. Finer cells are not automatically more accurate: they can expose uncertainty as broken walls while increasing memory and update cost.

Handle missing and maximum-range returns deliberately

In integrate_scan(), nonfinite ranges and ranges below the minimum are skipped. A finite value near the maximum range marks the ray as free without creating an occupied endpoint. Confusing a maximum-range miss with an obstacle makes an artificial ring around the sensor.

The implementation currently skips positive infinity. Some drivers use infinity for “no obstacle within range”; others use invalid values for failed sensing. If your bag uses infinity for valid clear rays, an explicit preprocessing rule could replace those values with the sensor’s maximum. Do not apply the same replacement blindly to NaNs: a failed measurement is not evidence of free space. Document the driver’s semantics before modifying this rule.

Coverage in the report is the fraction of cells whose stored log odds differ from the prior. It is a useful update indicator, not a proof of geometric accuracy or safe navigability. A bad transform can produce high coverage and a bad map.

Decide what the next system must estimate

If walls remain doubled with the correct sensor offset and valid timing, revisit the motion estimate. This mapper treats recorded odometry as truth and never corrects the robot trajectory. Wheel slip, radius error and integration error can therefore distort the map. In Lab 5, scan matching and loop constraints will help estimate the trajectory as well as the map.

Keep both maps, reports and one annotated region showing the defect or the limit of your comparison. Explain the chosen repair with a coordinate calculation and show one cell’s evidence history. Your result is a reproducible mapping investigation, not a requirement to make every pixel look clean.

Optional extension: interpolate x/y and wrapped yaw between neighbouring odometry headers. Compare only scans whose interpolation timestamps are bounded by valid samples, and report timing/error changes against nearest-neighbour matching.

References for this lab

  • Probabilistic Robotics, Thrun, Burgard and Fox: the occupancy-grid and inverse-sensor-model chapters explain the belief update used here.
  • Nav2 mapping and localisation setup: connects map generation to the navigation system that will consume it.
  • SLAM Toolbox maintainer documentation: preview the pose-graph approach that addresses the trajectory-estimation limitation exposed by this lab.

Lab 5: Build a reusable map, then find the robot inside it

Lab 4 drew the room using the robot’s estimated motion. Now separate two jobs: mapping builds a representation of the room; localisation estimates where the robot is in that room. A pose means position and orientation together. Even with a perfect saved map, a newly started robot still needs an estimate of its pose before it can use that map.

Two-hour mission: improve on the odometry-only map, save it, and start a new robot session that can localise against that saved evidence. You will distinguish the map itself from the robot’s belief about its position.

Spend 15 minutes on pose uncertainty, 30 mapping and saving, 30 localising, 30 building/testing the scan service and 15 saving the result. Use the shared terminal setup and retain your Lab 4 comparison images.

Two related questions: where is the room, and where am I?

Mapping estimates the surroundings. Localisation estimates the robot’s position and orientation within a map. That position and orientation together are its pose. SLAM, short for simultaneous localisation and mapping, estimates the robot’s trajectory and map together. It is useful when we do not begin with a complete map.

Wheel movement gives a useful estimate of travel, called odometry, but small errors accumulate. Recognising a place the robot has visited before can provide evidence to correct the estimate. Localisation methods also need to represent uncertainty: several candidate poses may fit a measurement. A particle in the later exercise is one candidate pose with a weight expressing its relative support. The arithmetic below shows how these weights are handled.

Explain why the previous map could bend

The Lab 4 mapper projected each beam using an odometry pose and never revised that pose. If the motion estimate drifts, observations of one physical wall land in different cells. SLAM means simultaneous localisation and mapping: estimate the robot’s path of poses, or trajectory, while constructing the map. Scan matching compares overlapping measured shapes to estimate motion between observations. It adds constraints from matching geometry; revisiting a place can add a loop constraint between poses recorded at different times.

SLAM Toolbox maintains a pose graph: vertices represent poses and edges encode constraints between them. Optimisation adjusts poses to make these constraints more consistent. It does not make every observation correct, and a repetitive corridor can still support an incorrect match. Today’s evidence must show what your route actually achieved, rather than assume every loop triggers a useful closure.

The frame chain separates responsibilities. odom -> base_footprint provides continuous local motion and may drift. map -> odom supplies a global correction from SLAM or localisation. The base’s map pose is their composition. A global correction can move the robot’s apparent map position without a discontinuity in the wheel-odometry trajectory.

Understand correction and uncertainty with small numbers

Imagine odometry reports the robot 2.0 m from its origin, but matching the map places it at 1.8 m along an aligned map axis. A translation correction of -0.2 m makes the two agree in this one-dimensional example. Rotations require rotating the displacement as well; adding x/y values alone works only when the axes align. map -> odom carries the correction so wheel odometry can stay locally smooth. The ROS frame convention assigns these roles to map and odom; neither frame name promises perfect measurements.

A pose graph expresses agreements and disagreements as errors called residuals. If an edge predicts 1.0 m separation but two estimated poses are 1.1 m apart, its distance residual is 0.1 m. An optimiser changes pose estimates to reduce a weighted combination of such errors. Weight represents how much that constraint should influence the estimate. Conflicting or incorrect constraints can still produce an incorrect solution.

For particles, weights express relative support, not a numbered ranking. Suppose three candidate poses have unnormalised weights 2, 1 and 1. Their sum is 4; dividing each by 4 gives probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. A candidate with weight 0.5 receives half the sampling probability, not a guarantee of correctness. Their effective sample size is 1/(0.5²+0.25²+0.25²), about 2.67. Three equal weights would give 3; one weight of 1 would give 1. This explains why the measure is about concentration, even though it has the units of a sample count.

Map one connected inspection route

Stop prior simulations and playback with Ctrl+C and arc-clean. Terminal A starts the simulator:

ros2 launch arc_gazebo simulation.launch.py headless:=true

Terminal B starts SLAM:

ros2 launch arc_nav slam.launch.py

Terminal C opens a map viewer:

arc-map-view

Alternatively use RViz:

rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix --share arc_nav)/rviz/slam.rviz" \
  --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

The lightweight viewer is useful on VMs with RViz map-rendering problems. A working map topic and a broken rendering window are different faults. Confirm data with ros2 topic info /map --verbose before changing SLAM settings.

Drive the robot in terminal D:

arc-drive --speed 0.2 --for 180

This driver follows available space and brakes for nearby obstacles. It does not guarantee complete exploration or a loop closure. Watch its route and stop it with Ctrl+C if you need to change strategy. Once it is closed, use keyboard teleoperation to revisit a distinctive corner and reconnect the route to a previously mapped area. Keep only one command source active.

Inspect arc_nav/config/slam_toolbox.yaml: identify the scan topic, base/odom/map frames and map resolution. These are interface and geometry assumptions, not arbitrary tuning values. Changing a frame name does not move a sensor. Increasing scan-matching effort cannot repair a scan whose frame is absent from TF.

Observe ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map odom while mapping. A change can reflect a global correction; by itself it is not proof of a specific loop-closure event. Pair it with the map/trajectory behaviour and relevant SLAM logs.

Save an artifact another process can use

Stop the driver, leaving SLAM and simulation running:

mkdir -p "$HOME/arc_ws/maps"
ros2 run nav2_map_server map_saver_cli \
  -f "$HOME/arc_ws/maps/slam_map" \
  --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true -p save_map_timeout:=10.0

Check the generated YAML and its image filename. Keep the pair together. A map image without its scale and origin loses the conversion from pixels to metres. Use a new stem for later map versions rather than silently replacing the map used by a previous navigation trial.

Compare one revisited wall with the Lab 4 result. The route may differ, so this is a qualitative comparison unless you replay the same bag through both pipelines. Record that distinction. For a matched optional replay, stop all live publishers, launch SLAM with simulation time, then use the filtered playback command from Lab 3.

Start again with a known map

Stop the simulator, SLAM and viewers, then run arc-clean. Start:

ros2 launch arc_lab5 localization.launch.py \
  map:="$HOME/arc_ws/maps/slam_map.yaml" headless:=true

This launch includes a new simulator, a map server that publishes the saved map, and AMCL (Adaptive Monte Carlo Localisation), which estimates robot pose against that map. It does not include RViz. In another terminal:

rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix --share arc_nav)/rviz/arc_navigation.rviz" \
  --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

Use 2D Pose Estimate to place the robot near its starting position in the saved map, dragging the arrow to set heading. Use the observed wall/corner geometry to choose that pose. Do not automatically type Gazebo’s spawn coordinates as map coordinates; Lab 3 already showed that frame origins can differ.

Some ROS components have named operating states, called a lifecycle. “Configured” means resources have been prepared; active means the component has been enabled to do its job. This launch manages startup for you. The first command below checks AMCL’s state; the others inspect its pose and transform:

ros2 lifecycle get /amcl
ros2 topic echo /amcl_pose --once
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map base_footprint

The pose message also has a covariance array. Covariance describes uncertainty and how errors in different quantities vary together. A diagonal position variance of 0.04 m² corresponds to a standard deviation of 0.2 m because sqrt(0.04)=0.2. A small reported variance is the estimator’s belief, not an independent accuracy measurement. Use scan alignment as additional evidence.

After stopping the echo, move slowly a short distance with teleoperation. The laser points should align with the saved walls. AMCL may wait for configured translation/rotation thresholds before incorporating another update, so an unchanging stationary estimate is not automatically a stalled process. Keep SLAM stopped: AMCL now owns the map -> odom correction.

Build a service for checking one input to localisation

A topic continuously streams data. A service handles a request and returns one response. Use a service for a short check, such as asking whether a recent, valid front-sector scan exists. A navigation mission takes time and needs progress/cancellation, so we will use an action for that in Lab 6.

While AMCL is running, inspect the available interfaces:

ros2 service list -t
ros2 param list /amcl
ros2 param get /amcl base_frame_id
ros2 interface show std_srvs/srv/Trigger

A service definition has request fields above --- and response fields below. Trigger has an empty request and a response with success and message. We can use this standard type without generating a custom interface package. Write scan_service.py in your student package, reusing front_min() from Lab 3:

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from std_srvs.srv import Trigger
from robot_workshop.front_range import front_min


class ScanService(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('scan_service')
        self.last_stamp = None
        self.last_valid = False
        self.subscription = self.create_subscription(
            LaserScan, '/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.service = self.create_service(Trigger, 'check_scan', self.on_check)

    def on_scan(self, scan):
        value = front_min(scan.ranges, scan.angle_min, scan.angle_increment,
                          scan.range_min, scan.range_max)
        self.last_valid = math.isfinite(value)
        self.last_stamp = scan.header.stamp.sec + scan.header.stamp.nanosec * 1e-9

    def on_check(self, request, response):
        now = self.get_clock().now().nanoseconds * 1e-9
        age = None if self.last_stamp is None else now - self.last_stamp
        response.success = bool(self.last_valid and age is not None and 0 <= age < 0.5)
        response.message = 'No scan yet' if age is None else f'Scan age: {age:.3f} s'
        return response


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = ScanService()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

The subscription stores information from each scan. The service callback checks that stored information when asked; it does not wait inside the callback for a new scan. Such a wait could prevent the subscription callback from running in this simple single-threaded arrangement. Returning promptly keeps the node responsive.

A ROS timestamp has whole seconds and nanoseconds. There are one billion nanoseconds in a second, hence multiplication by 1e-9. Age is current time minus measurement time. Our criterion is valid numeric data with age from zero up to, but not including, 0.5 seconds. A negative age suggests inconsistent clocks or a time jump, so it does not pass.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/scan_service.py and add 'scan_service = robot_workshop.scan_service:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Add <exec_depend>std_srvs</exec_depend> to package.xml. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

Start your server with the simulator’s time reference:

ros2 run robot_workshop scan_service --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true

Call it in a second prepared terminal:

ros2 service type /check_scan
ros2 service call /check_scan std_srvs/srv/Trigger '{}'

The braces represent an empty request. Expect success: true when recent valid front-sector rays exist. This checks a scan input only; it does not prove that AMCL is active, that the map is correct, or that TF connects the sensor.

Stop only this server and restart it with --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true -r /scan:=/missing_scan. The same service call should now return false with ‘No scan yet’. Restore its original input and verify recovery. If simulation time itself is paused, the measured age also stops increasing. Lab 10 introduces a steady-clock watchdog for a different purpose: detecting a producer that has stopped sending commands in real time.

You can use this pattern in your own project: subscribe to changing state, retain the information needed for a short decision, and expose a service with an explicit response. The official service tutorial shows how a Python client calls such a server asynchronously.

Look inside the estimate: several possible robot poses

Open starters/lab05/particle_filter.py. A particle is a candidate (x,y,theta). Rather than trusting only one guess, the algorithm keeps many candidates and gives more influence to candidates whose predicted measurements agree with the sensor. Here theta is heading. Read the three function roles first; modifying the particle-filter implementation is an optional extension to today’s live mapping/localisation mission.

predict() applies an odometry increment with noise, spreading plausible poses. update_weights() gives better agreement with a measurement more weight. resample() draws a new population from those weights. Its systematic sampling procedure preserves high-weight regions without requiring every particle to be identical.

This figure uses a small landmark-range measurement model to isolate the weighting mechanism. It is not an AMCL lidar run. The helper computes predicted ranges from each candidate pose, compares them with synthetic measured ranges, then passes the error to the reference filter. AMCL’s configured likelihood-field model instead scores laser endpoints against mapped obstacles.

Effective sample size 1/sum(weights**2) indicates how concentrated the weights are. A low value motivates resampling; it does not certify that the surviving hypotheses are correct. The starter’s weight routine normalises the current likelihoods directly, so it is a teaching mechanism rather than a complete general-purpose recursive Bayesian filter. Read those implementation choices before claiming to have reproduced AMCL.

Recover from an uncertain initial pose

Save your correctly aligned view first. Then, while stationary, give AMCL a nearby but visibly imperfect initial pose, such as a small heading error near a distinctive corner. Observe whether a short turn and translation improve scan alignment. If the estimate stays in the wrong corridor, use the evidence to reinitialise near a recognisable location.

The practical problem is to provide a plausible initial belief and informative observations. Increasing particle count without addressing ambiguous geometry can spend more computation on the same ambiguity. Reducing motion noise until the cloud looks narrow can make the filter unable to represent actual drift. Record the change that repaired your case and the scan alignment supporting it.

Keep the saved map pair, a before/after localisation image, the initial-pose procedure, and a note identifying the current owner of map -> odom. This is the starting state for Lab 6. Stop teleoperation before the navigation mission.

  • Probabilistic Robotics: use the Monte Carlo localisation chapters to relate prediction, weighting and resampling to your code.
