Lab 6: Deliver a navigation goal through free space

In Lab 5 you gave the robot a map and an estimate of where it is. Now you give it a destination. Navigation is the process of choosing a route and producing motion to reach that destination while accounting for obstacles. Nav2 is the ROS 2 navigation software we will use to connect these jobs.

Two-hour mission: use the saved warehouse map to reach a chosen destination, then diagnose how planning and local control contribute to the result. Your first repeat keeps the map, start, goal and controller fixed. An optional later comparison changes only the controller.

Allow 20 minutes for startup and localisation, 20 for a first goal, 40 for your action client, 25 for a repeat and costmap diagnosis, and 15 to save the result. The search-algorithm and second-controller comparisons are optional extensions after one complete mission works. Bring the Lab 5 map and use Start here.

From a destination to wheel commands

Giving a robot a destination does not specify every movement along the way. A planner chooses a route through the map. A controller repeatedly chooses motion commands to follow that route using current information. A costmap gives locations costs that help navigation prefer usable space and avoid obstacles. Cost is a numerical planning penalty, not money.

Nav2 is the ROS 2 navigation software we will use. Its navigation action server accepts a goal pose and coordinates work toward it. Your action client requests that goal and receives progress and the eventual outcome. Revisit topics, services and actions if the word action is new. Today you will follow one goal through those stages and build the client that requests it.

Start a complete navigation session

The planner chooses a path across the map. The controller repeatedly chooses velocities to follow that path. A server is a node offering one of these jobs to other components. A costmap assigns costs to locations so planning/control can account for occupied cells and distance from obstacles. You will first see these parts working together, then inspect them separately.

Stop the Lab 5 session and run arc-clean. Terminal A:

ros2 launch arc_gazebo simulation.launch.py headless:=true

Terminal B:

ros2 launch arc_nav navigation.launch.py \
  map:="$HOME/arc_ws/maps/slam_map.yaml" params:=dwb

This navigation launch starts localisation, navigation servers and RViz. It does not start a simulator, which is why terminal A is separate. Set 2D Pose Estimate in RViz as in Lab 5 and wait until the scan agrees with the saved map. Check the servers in terminal C:

ros2 lifecycle get /amcl
ros2 lifecycle get /planner_server
ros2 lifecycle get /controller_server
ros2 action list -t
ros2 topic info /cmd_vel --verbose

An active server is ready to perform its role; it is not proof that its inputs are correct. Confirm localisation and transforms before sending a goal. Ensure teleoperation and arc-drive are stopped so command publishers do not compete.

Watch one goal pass through the system

Choose a reachable free-space point with room for the robot to turn at the end. Use Nav2 Goal in RViz, dragging to choose the final heading. Observe the global path, the robot’s local motion and the final orientation adjustment. Record the selected pose in map coordinates so you can repeat the trial.

The action /navigate_to_pose accepts a stamped pose in a named frame and returns feedback while work proceeds. An action is a ROS interface for a job that takes time: a client sends a goal, receives progress feedback and eventually gets a result; it can also request cancellation. RViz is the client when you click Nav2 Goal. This is different from a topic’s ongoing stream of readings. The navigator coordinates a planner to compute a path and a controller to generate velocities that follow it. A path is a geometric proposal; the controller must still respond to current obstacles, velocity limits and the robot’s motion.

For a scripted repeat, substitute your observed free-space coordinates for GOAL_X and GOAL_Y. The example orientation below requests zero yaw:

ros2 action send_goal /navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose \
  "{pose: {header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: GOAL_X, y: GOAL_Y}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" \
  --feedback

This is a template: the two capitalised placeholders must become numbers before running it. Inspect ros2 interface show nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose to see the goal, result and feedback fields. Do not regard a printed “goal accepted” as a completed delivery. Record the final action result and any recovery behaviour.

Build the action client that sends your mission

Your own project needs a program that requests navigation and handles its outcome. It should not depend on a person clicking RViz for every delivery. Use the goal you already verified, then create send_goal.py in your package.

A future represents a result that is not available yet. Sending the goal first gives a future for acceptance and a goal handle. An accepted handle then provides a separate future for the final result. Feedback can arrive while that result is pending. The executor must keep processing events for these responses to be received, which is why the program spins while it waits.

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.action import ActionClient
from nav2_msgs.action import NavigateToPose
from action_msgs.msg import GoalStatus


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = Node('student_goal_client')
    node.declare_parameter('x', 0.0)
    node.declare_parameter('y', 0.0)
    node.declare_parameter('yaw', 0.0)
    client = ActionClient(node, NavigateToPose, '/navigate_to_pose')
    handle = None
    try:
        if not client.wait_for_server(timeout_sec=10.0):
            node.get_logger().error('Navigation action server is unavailable')
            return
        # Let a subscribed simulation clock update before stamping the goal.
        rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=1.0)
        x, y, yaw = [float(node.get_parameter(name).value) for name in ('x', 'y', 'yaw')]
        if not all(math.isfinite(value) for value in (x, y, yaw)):
            raise ValueError('Goal coordinates and yaw must be finite')
        goal = NavigateToPose.Goal()
        goal.pose.header.frame_id = 'map'
        goal.pose.header.stamp = node.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        goal.pose.pose.position.x = x
        goal.pose.pose.position.y = y
        goal.pose.pose.orientation.z = math.sin(yaw / 2)
        goal.pose.pose.orientation.w = math.cos(yaw / 2)

        def feedback(message):
            remaining = message.feedback.distance_remaining
            node.get_logger().info(f'Remaining path: {remaining:.2f} m')

        future = client.send_goal_async(goal, feedback_callback=feedback)
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, future)
        handle = future.result()
        if handle is None or not handle.accepted:
            node.get_logger().warning('Goal rejected')
            return
        result_future = handle.get_result_async()
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, result_future)
        result = result_future.result()
        if result is not None:
            success = result.status == GoalStatus.STATUS_SUCCEEDED
            node.get_logger().info(f'Finished: success={success}, status={result.status}')
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        if handle is not None and rclpy.ok():
            cancel = handle.cancel_goal_async()
            rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, cancel, timeout_sec=2.0)
    finally:
        client.destroy()
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

The target has a frame, timestamp, position and orientation. yaw measures heading around the upward z axis. A quaternion represents a 3D orientation with four numbers (x,y,z,w) whose squared values sum to 1. For a flat robot with roll and pitch zero, the required form is (0,0,sin(yaw/2),cos(yaw/2)). At zero yaw this gives (0,0,0,1); at a 90-degree left turn, z and w are each about 0.707. You can use this restricted formula without deriving general 3D rotation algebra today.

The action status tells us whether navigation succeeded, aborted or was cancelled. Acceptance only says the server agreed to attempt the goal. distance_remaining is navigation feedback, not an independent measurement of collision risk. The server can abort after initially accepting a request.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/send_goal.py and add 'send_goal = robot_workshop.send_goal:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Add nav2_msgs and action_msgs as exec_depend entries in package.xml. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

With the healthy Lab 6 simulator/Nav2 session active and localised, enter the coordinates of your verified goal when prompted:

read -r -p 'Verified goal x in map metres: ' goal_x
read -r -p 'Verified goal y in map metres: ' goal_y
ros2 run robot_workshop send_goal --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true \
  -p x:="$goal_x" -p y:="$goal_y" -p yaw:=0.0

Enter decimals such as 1.0, using your own reachable coordinates. read stores text in a shell variable, and $goal_x inserts that text in the next command. Quoting preserves it as one argument. The parameter names are those you explicitly declared in your node, not hidden features of Nav2.

Run one reachable goal to completion, then run a second and cancel it through RViz. Record the final status for each. A cancellation request also takes time; its acknowledgement and the final cancelled result are distinct events. The client attempts cancellation on an interrupt when its ROS context is still active, but Ctrl+C can shut that context down first. Use RViz to cancel a goal before closing the client. Killing a client process is not a reliable substitute for cancelling the server’s work.

To extend this into a delivery sequence, put the next request after the previous result and advance only on success. For a failed request, report the failure or invoke a bounded recovery policy. Do not send all destinations at once and assume they form a queue; a new goal can change the server’s current task.

See the Python action tutorial for the future/handle pattern and the Jazzy action definition for the exact fields used by this installed ROS release.

Explain the space the planner is searching

The saved occupancy map describes what mapping observed. A costmap combines that information with current obstacle observations and inflation. The global costmap supports route selection in map; the local costmap follows the robot in odom and supports short-horizon control. These frame choices preserve continuous local control while localisation applies global corrections.

Inflation gives obstacles a surrounding cost field. A path close to a wall may be legal but expensive. This differs from simply enlarging every obstacle into a binary forbidden region. Robot footprint checking and inflation preferences have related but distinct jobs.

Read the global_costmap and local_costmap blocks in arc_nav/config/nav2_dwb.yaml. Locate the static, obstacle and inflation layers, their frames, the robot radius and scan topic. Then read starters/lab06/grid_tools.py. Its inflate() function grows a binary obstacle mask by a disc; it is an understandable approximation for a point-grid planner, not an exact implementation of Nav2’s graded cost field.

The helper reshapes an OccupancyGrid as (height, width), because ROS stores it in row-major order. The message’s -1..100 display encoding is different from Nav2’s internal cost values. grid_to_world() adds half a cell to return the cell centre. world_to_grid() now uses mathematical floor, so a point just below the origin stays outside the first cell. Still check the returned bounds before array indexing: NumPy interprets a negative index from the array’s end. These helpers assume map axes aligned with world axes, as in our exported maps; a rotated map origin would also require undoing its rotation. These details determine whether the path lies where the drawing says it does.

Solve a blocked-route discrepancy

If RViz shows an apparently open passage but the planner refuses it, compare the occupancy map, the inflated costmap and the robot footprint. An opening wide enough for a point may be too narrow for a 0.22 m radius robot plus margin. Unknown cells may also be blocked by your chosen planning policy.

Optional search investigation: use the existing offline comparison to isolate search logic from live sensing. Complete your live goal first:

python3 starters/algorithms/compare.py --moves 4 \
  --figures results/lab06_four_connected
python3 starters/algorithms/compare.py --moves 8 \
  --figures results/lab06_eight_connected

A grid search treats free cells as vertices and legal moves as edges. In four-connected movement, an interior cell can move up, down, left or right. Eight-connected movement also permits diagonals, subject to the implementation’s corner checks. An edge’s cost is the distance or penalty assigned to that move.

For cells separated by two columns and one row, Manhattan distance is |2|+|1|=3 straight steps. If diagonals cost sqrt(2), one diagonal plus one straight move costs about 2.414. A heuristic of 3 would overestimate that unobstructed eight-connected route. sqrt(2) follows from the Pythagorean rule: a diagonal across a unit square has length sqrt(1²+1²).

A* orders candidates using f=g+h: g is the cost already paid from the start, and h estimates the cost still needed. A shortest-path guarantee requires appropriate assumptions, including nonnegative edge costs, a suitable heuristic and correct handling of revisited states. It is not a guarantee for any function someone names astar.

Read one map’s table alongside its path. Breadth-first search (BFS) minimises edge count when edges have equal cost. With diagonal steps costing square-root-of-two, step count and metric cost are different objectives. Dijkstra uses accumulated cost; A* adds a heuristic estimate. An octile-distance heuristic suits these eight-connected costs, while Manhattan distance can overestimate them. A heuristic is an estimate of remaining cost that helps guide the search. Depth-first search (DFS) is useful for understanding traversal but does not promise a shortest route. Read the algorithm trace on one small map before comparing the full table.

Use this investigation to propose a repair supported by the actual failure: choose a goal in confirmed free space, correct the footprint, or revise an excessively conservative margin. Do not reduce collision geometry simply to make a failed path appear. Save the map/costmap views that show why your change was appropriate.

Optional extension: compare controller behaviour fairly

DWB, our first local-controller plugin, samples candidate velocity commands, predicts short trajectories and scores them using critics, functions that evaluate obstacle, path and goal behaviour. Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control samples control sequences, evaluates trajectories and updates a control sequence using their costs. Both depend on their model, constraints and configuration. Neither is guaranteed to win on every warehouse route.

Read both nav2_dwb.yaml and nav2_mppi.yaml before the trial and record any configuration differences relevant to your experiment. Stop both launch terminals, run arc-clean, and restart the simulator from the same world. Launch navigation with params:=mppi, initialise the same map pose and send the same goal. Restarting only Nav2 would leave the robot at the previous endpoint and invalidate the start-state comparison.

For each controller, keep the action outcome, route, elapsed time with the clock identified, observed recoveries and any contact. Repeat the matched mission if time permits. Report a small number of trials as a classroom comparison, not a reliable ranking of controller quality. A shorter failed run is not better than a slower successful delivery.

The repository’s ROS evaluation adapter does not implement a complete world-reset service. Changing a seed in that adapter is therefore insufficient to prove identical physical initial states. These lab trials explicitly restart the simulator and verify the pose; Lab 9 will use a fast simulator with an executable reset contract for larger comparisons.

Carry forward a healthy mission

For the core lab, repeat your known-reachable goal with the same controller after restarting from the recorded pose. Explain which part chose the path and which part generated motion. A successful first run followed by a successful repeat is enough to carry the mission into Lab 7; complete the optional comparisons when time allows.

Save one successful goal and its map/start/configuration so Lab 7 can deliberately break that same mission. Your report should connect the chosen route to the costmap and the executed motion to the controller. If a failure remains, preserve its logs and identify the last verified stage in the data/command chain.

Optional startup investigation: after stopping navigation, run ros2 run arc_lab1 managed_beacon in one terminal. In another, use ros2 lifecycle set /managed_beacon configure, then activate, then deactivate. Observe /beacon with ros2 topic echo /beacon while doing so. Resources can exist while a component is inactive; activation starts publication. This small example isolates the startup states you inspected on the Nav2 servers. Stop the beacon and observer afterwards.

References for this lab

  • Nav2 navigation concepts: connect the live servers and action to their roles.
  • Nav2 tuning guide: use the costmap and controller discussion to justify one measured change.
  • Open-Source, Cost-Aware Kinematically Feasible Planning for Mobile and Surface Robotics (2024; revised 2025): a research view of planning costs and motion constraints beyond a binary classroom grid.

Lab 7: Recover a mission that stops making progress

Last time the robot reached a destination. Today it may still have a valid path but fail to get there. Progress means useful movement towards completing the mission; recovery is an attempt to restore that movement after a problem. We will change one speed setting, watch the effect and repair the cause before examining the more detailed recovery structure.

Two-hour mission: take the working delivery from Lab 6, diagnose a deliberate slow-motion fault, and explain when retrying helps and when it should end. You will use live evidence to separate a planner failure from a controller or progress-checking failure.

Use 20 minutes to reproduce the mission, 25 to isolate the fault, 30 to build your retry rule, 30 to repair and repeat, and 15 to record the explanation. Bring the Lab 5 map and Lab 6 start/goal record. Apply the shared terminal setup.

A program can be running while the mission is stuck

A robot might still send messages while making no useful progress. We need a rule for deciding whether it has moved far enough within a period of time. We also need to decide what to try after a failure and when to stop retrying.

A behaviour tree arranges decisions and tasks so that their outcomes determine what happens next. A task can report running, success or failure. A recovery is an attempt to resolve a problem before retrying useful work. A retry budget limits the number of attempts. These terms describe decision logic, not a guarantee that a recovery will succeed. We will use measurements to distinguish a communication fault from a motion or planning problem.

Start the same mission with one injected defect

Stop all prior sessions and run arc-clean:

ros2 launch arc_lab7 difficult_robot.launch.py scenario:=1 \
  map:="$HOME/arc_ws/maps/slam_map.yaml" headless:=true

This launch includes the simulator, Nav2 and RViz. Do not start another simulator. After approximately 25 wall seconds it attempts to set DWB’s FollowPath.max_vel_x to 0.02 m/s. Initialise the map pose, then verify that the fault actually took effect:

ros2 param get /controller_server FollowPath.max_vel_x
ros2 param get /controller_server progress_checker.required_movement_radius
ros2 param get /controller_server progress_checker.movement_time_allowance

If the first value is still the healthy value because startup took longer than the timer, wait for /controller_server to be active and apply the fault:

ros2 run arc_lab7 fault_injector --ros-args -p scenario:=1

Check the value again. A launch script printing its intended fault is not proof that the parameter service accepted it. Send the same known-reachable goal used in Lab 6, then observe the path and actual movement.

Locate the failure by following evidence

A visible global path means a planning request produced a route; it says nothing about the maximum speed allowed during execution. Inspect command and feedback while the mission runs:

ros2 topic info /cmd_vel --verbose
ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel --once
ros2 topic echo /odom --once
ros2 lifecycle get /controller_server

Compare the forward velocity command with odometry’s measured forward velocity. If the command is small and feedback follows it, the wheels are doing what they were asked. If the command is normal but feedback remains near zero, investigate the relay, controller state and simulated contacts. If commands are absent, check action/server state and transforms. These distinctions prevent changing the planner when the limit is actually in the controller.

The configured progress checker requires 0.5 m of movement within 10 s. At a maximum forward speed of 0.02 m/s, even ideal straight motion covers only 0.2 m in that interval. This makes the injected limit inconsistent with the progress criterion. The observed recovery timing also depends on the path, scheduling and server state, so preserve the actual log rather than promising an exact failure second.

Read the decision logic rather than memorising recovery names

First describe the decision in ordinary language: keep a short history of positions; if the robot stays in a small area for too long, flag it as stuck. Try a recovery, watch for renewed progress, and stop retrying after a defined limit. The Python classes below make each part of that description explicit.

Open starters/lab07/recovery.py. StuckDetector stores a sliding window of positions and compares the latest position with the oldest. It uses displacement, not total distance travelled. A robot oscillating in a doorway can accumulate path length while making almost no net progress.

python3 - <<'PY'
from starters.lab07.recovery import StuckDetector, RecoveryEscalator
detector = StuckDetector(window_s=5.0, min_displacement_m=0.15)
for k in range(120):
    stuck = detector.update(0.02 * k * 0.05, 0.0)
print('slow run classified stuck:', stuck)
recovery = RecoveryEscalator()
print([recovery.next_action().value for _ in range(9)])
recovery.on_progress()
print('after progress:', recovery.next_action().value)
PY

Expect the slow trajectory to be classified stuck after the history fills. The escalator produces two cycles of clear, spin, wait and back-up, then aborts; on_progress() resets its cycle position so an unrelated later blockage starts with the first recovery again. This Python model illustrates bounded escalation; its thresholds and retry count differ from the live Nav2 configuration.

An in-place turn is intentionally low displacement but may be valid near the goal. A useful detector therefore needs context: which behaviour is active, whether translation is currently expected, and how long that behaviour should take. A single distance threshold cannot describe every healthy robot action.

Build a bounded decision rule before connecting it to motion

A recovery rule is easier to check when its decision is a pure function of known inputs. Build the displacement calculation and a retry budget in progress.py. This small program will become a decision component for your Lab 6 client; it does not directly publish wheel commands.

import math


def displacement(start, end):
    dx = end[0] - start[0]
    dy = end[1] - start[1]
    return math.hypot(dx, dy)


class RetryBudget:
    def __init__(self, limit=2):
        if limit < 0:
            raise ValueError('Retry limit cannot be negative')
        self.limit = limit
        self.used = 0

    def decide(self, made_progress):
        if made_progress:
            self.used = 0
            return 'continue'
        if self.used >= self.limit:
            return 'abort'
        self.used += 1
        return 'retry'


def main():
    budget = RetryBudget(limit=2)
    for end in [(0.01, 0), (0.02, 0), (0.03, 0), (0.3, 0)]:
        distance = displacement((0, 0), end)
        print(distance, budget.decide(distance >= 0.15))

hypot(dx,dy) calculates sqrt(dx²+dy²), the straight-line distance between two positions. From (0,0) to (0.3,0.4) m it gives 0.5 m. Walking around a loop can increase travelled path length while returning displacement to zero. Before calling a robot stuck, also check that translation was actually expected.

An object retains used between decisions. With a limit of two, the first two failed progress checks request retries and the third requests abort. A successful progress check resets the history. The sample’s last input illustrates resetting for a subsequent observation; it does not automatically resurrect an aborted live navigation action.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/progress.py and add 'progress = robot_workshop.progress:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

ros2 run robot_workshop progress

Expect decisions retry, retry, abort, continue. This executable is an ordinary Python program, so it will not appear in ros2 node list. ros2 run starts an installed executable; creating a Node is what makes software participate in the ROS graph.

Add a boundary case at exactly 0.15 m and decide whether it counts as progress. The sample uses >=, so it does. Then change the limit to one and predict the new decision sequence before running. To connect this rule to your action client, store consecutive odometry positions over a stated time window, check whether movement was expected, and request cancellation before deciding to send another goal. Record that integration as a small flow of states: goal active, cancel pending, retry allowed, finished. The pure decision component you built is complete; the automatic action integration is an extension.

For parameter experiments, learn the generic persistence tools:

mkdir -p ~/student_ws/config_snapshots
ros2 param dump /controller_server > ~/student_ws/config_snapshots/controller_before.yaml

> writes command output to a file, replacing that filename if it exists. Choose a new filename for later snapshots. This is a parameter snapshot, not a recording of the whole navigation state. ros2 param load NODE FILE requests runtime changes, which the node may reject; supplying a parameter file at startup is a separate mechanism. Save a snapshot before tuning and verify each changed value with ros2 param get. See the ROS parameter guide.

Trace the behaviour tree that coordinates actions

You have already seen an if condition decide whether a range warning appears. A behaviour tree organises a larger set of decisions and actions, such as “try navigation; if it fails, attempt recovery; then try again.” It is ticked repeatedly so a long action can remain in progress across many checks. Start by tracing that outer decision; the individual XML node names are details to read as you reach them.

Read arc_nav/behavior_trees/arc_recovery.xml. A behaviour-tree node returns RUNNING, SUCCESS or FAILURE; the parent uses that status to decide what to tick next. The file’s PipelineSequence connects path computation and following, with a rate controller limiting replanning requests. The outer RecoveryNode can invoke recovery and retry after a navigation failure.

The recovery branch tries clearing costmaps, spinning, waiting and backing up. Clearing can remove stale observations, but current sensors can mark the same obstacle again immediately. Waiting can help with a temporary obstruction; it cannot change a permanent speed limit. Backing up changes the physical situation and requires free space behind the robot.

The XML file is an available example, not evidence that it is the active tree. The baseline configuration does not explicitly select this file. For the core lab, diagnose the running default tree through the action/logs and use the example to understand its control structure. If you test an edited tree as an extension, pass its absolute filename in the action’s behavior_tree field and verify loading in the navigator logs. Merely editing an unused XML file cannot change the running mission.

Repair the cause, then check that the mission can finish

Cancel the current goal through RViz before changing the limit:

ros2 param set /controller_server FollowPath.max_vel_x 0.5
ros2 param get /controller_server FollowPath.max_vel_x

Retry a reachable goal and inspect command magnitude, odometry and final action result. To make a matched comparison with the original route, stop the fault launch, run arc-clean and restart the healthy Lab 6 simulator/navigation pair from the recorded initial pose. The repaired live parameter disappears at restart unless you also change the source configuration; here the source configuration was healthy, so no persistent edit is necessary.

Do not “repair” this fault by allowing endless recovery or by deleting the progress checker. That would allow a failed mission to remain running while concealing the incompatible speed/mission requirement. A deliberate low-speed application would instead need a justified progress policy consistent with its speed and acceptable completion time.

Check where a protective command actually goes

The speed-fault diagnosis and repaired mission complete the core investigation. The following command-path inspection is an extension for students who finish early, or preparation for a project involving a collision monitor.

Inspect the collision-monitor configuration and the command graph with ros2 node list, ros2 node info and ros2 topic info --verbose. A parameter block in YAML does not prove that a node was launched or that its output lies on the path to the wheels. Trace producer topic, any smoother/monitor inputs, their outputs, the relay and the controller subscription.

Scenario 3 in the supplied injector attempts to change a collision-monitor parameter; its effect depends on the monitor being active and on its configured zone type. Treat it as an optional graph/configuration investigation, not a guaranteed “robot stops” demonstration. The live chain is the evidence.

Finish with one causal report: the original healthy mission, the accepted fault value, the observed symptoms, the violated progress expectation, the repair and the repeated outcome. Include a bounded-abort policy for a genuine obstruction that cannot be cleared. This record becomes a useful baseline when learned control is introduced: an unfamiliar controller should not inherit unlimited authority simply because another controller got stuck.

References for this lab

  • Nav2 collision monitor configuration: verify input/output topics and zone types before interpreting a parameter change.

Lab 8: Make navigation an executable learning problem

So far a programmer chose the rules that turn observations into motion. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers another approach: an agent tries actions, receives feedback about the outcomes and improves its decision rule over many attempts. Today we build understanding of the task it will practise. We do not train a neural network until Lab 9.

Two-hour mission: run the same kind of obstacle-and-goal task inside a fast learning environment, inspect every interface value, and decide whether an episode ends for the right reason. The deliverable is an actual trajectory and a checked observation/action contract, before any neural network is trained.

Spend 20 minutes on the warehouse rollout, 25 on its numeric interface, 40 building your approach environment, 25 on ending conditions and 10 on results. Use the shared terminal setup, then stop Gazebo/Nav2 to free VM resources. These experiments need Python, NumPy, Gymnasium and Matplotlib; the course VM supplies them. No ROS node is launched by the commands below.

A learning problem still needs a program that defines the task

In reinforcement learning, an agent chooses an action from the information it receives. The environment calculates what happens next. It returns an observation, meaning information available to the agent, and a reward, meaning a number that scores the immediate outcome according to our design. A policy is the rule the agent uses to choose actions. An episode is one attempt, from reset until an ending condition.

Gymnasium defines a standard Python interface for this interaction. It is not Gazebo and does not automatically supply this course’s robot physics. Here a small environment implements the motion and obstacle rules. Today we inspect and build environments; training the policy comes in Lab 9. A good first check is whether a known action produces the movement and ending condition we expected.

Run first, inspect the path, then read the loop

A policy is a rule for choosing an action from an observation. It can be handwritten or learned. An environment simulates what happens after the action and returns the next observation and a numeric reward. An episode is one attempt from a starting state until success, collision or a time limit.

Gymnasium supplies a standard Python interface for environments. Our FastNavEnv implements that interface with a simple two-dimensional simulation; it is a separate simulator from Gazebo. We use it because training needs many repeated attempts. A rollout is the recorded sequence from one such attempt. Here the first policy is a supplied handwritten gap follower that tries to choose open space in the general direction of the goal.

The seed 500 is an integer used to reproduce a particular generated layout and random sequence. Keep it fixed when repeating this first run:

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy gap --seeds 500 \
  --out results/lab08_gap
xdg-open results/lab08_gap/trajectory_500.png

The plot shows the actual robot-centre path produced by this run, the start/end positions and goals. trajectory_500.csv stores time, pose and applied body velocities; episodes.csv and summary.json report the outcome. A dashed moving obstacle outline, if present, marks its initial position rather than its full motion history. The static plot is a result viewer, not a Gazebo screenshot.

Open teaching/rollout.py, arc_rl/nav_core.py and arc_rl/baselines.py together. The helper calls reset(seed=500), asks the gap-following policy for an action, calls step(action), records the resulting state and repeats until termination or truncation. It creates a fresh environment and controller for each episode. This simple loop makes the control problem executable and repeatable.

The fast environment integrates planar motion and raycasts against segments and circles. It makes sample collection inexpensive enough for training, but it does not simulate wheel slip, motor dynamics or the complete ROS message path. Similar observation shapes do not prove similar dynamics.

Inspect the contract the policy actually receives

Decode the numbers before using them

A vector is an ordered list of numbers; a scalar is one number. Encoding a 6.06 m beam with the warehouse bounds gives (6.06-0.12)/(12-0.12)=0.5. Normalisation puts different physical quantities on manageable numeric scales; it does not remove their meanings. To decode, multiply by 11.88 and add 0.12.

For planar motion, speed times time gives travel distance. Resolve that distance along x/y with cosine/sine of heading. Euler integration uses the heading at the start of the small step. During a turn the heading changes within the step, so this is approximate. At 0.5 m/s and 0.05 s, the centre travels about 0.025 m per step; compare that with obstacle sizes before enlarging the timestep.

The policy does not receive a screen image or the simulator’s full internal state. It receives a short numeric observation: ranges, goal direction and distance, and velocities. The contract is our agreement about the array’s size, order, units and scaling. Check those properties before trying to learn from the array; a network cannot repair a field silently put in the wrong slot.

python3 - <<'PY'
from arc_rl.nav_core import FastNavEnv, OBS
from arc_rl.arenas import training_scenario
env = FastNavEnv(scenario_factory=training_scenario, randomise_start=False)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=500)
print('shape / dtype:', obs.shape, obs.dtype)
print('inside declared space:', env.observation_space.contains(obs))
print('beam range:', float(obs[:OBS.n_beams].min()), float(obs[:OBS.n_beams].max()))
print('goal and velocity fields:', obs[OBS.n_beams:])
print(info)
env.close()
PY

Expect 29 float32 values. Interpret them using the actual index contract:

Indices Quantity Encoding
0-23 24 laser ranges (range - 0.12) / (12.0 - 0.12) after clipping
24 Distance to current goal min(distance, 20) / 20
25-26 Goal bearing in robot frame Sine and cosine
27 Current forward velocity Divided by 0.50 m/s
28 Current angular velocity Divided by 1.80 rad/s

A policy trained on this ordering cannot be given an array with cosine and sine swapped just because it has the same length. Units, clipping, beam order and frame meaning are part of the interface too. Sine/cosine avoids representing nearly identical headings just below +pi and just above -pi as distant numbers.

downsample_scan() divides raw beams into sectors and takes each sector’s minimum. A thin obstacle visible in one beam should survive aggregation; averaging could conceal it. The surrogate directly raycasts 24 directions, which is an approximation to the statistics of minimum pooling over a 360-beam sensor. This is already one specific transfer difference to record for Lab 10.

The current preprocessing replaces nonfinite values with maximum range. That keeps arrays finite but interprets missing readings optimistically. For a real sensor, distinguish a valid no-return reading from a failed observation and decide whether to stop, hold a previous sample briefly or mark the observation invalid. Do not silently train the network to regard every sensor failure as clear space.

Trace an action into the next state

In this task an action is a pair of numbers requesting forward and turning speed. This use of the word “action” belongs to the RL loop; it is not the ROS goal/feedback/result interface introduced in Lab 6.

The action has two values in [-1,1]. scale_action() maps the first to forward speed and the second to angular speed:

python3 - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from arc_rl.nav_core import scale_action
for a in ([1, 0], [-1, 0], [0.4, 0.5]):
    print(a, '->', scale_action(np.array(a, dtype=np.float32)))
PY

The outputs should be (0.5, 0), (-0.125, 0) and approximately (0.2, 0.9) in m/s and rad/s. Reverse is deliberately slower than forward. Multiplying every linear action by 0.5 would violate this contract for negative actions.

step() advances the pose for 0.05 s using the applied velocity, moves dynamic obstacles, computes clearance, checks the goal, calculates reward and returns a new observation. Unlike Lab 2’s exact-arc helper, this environment uses a simple Euler position update. At the fixed small timestep that is a deliberate approximation; increasing the timestep changes both numerical error and the distance the robot can travel between collision checks.

The environment’s geometric collision check subtracts the 0.22 m footprint radius from distance to obstacles. This is different from a laser distance to a surface. A positive beam value can still coexist with a colliding robot body. Read _clearance() before using beam distance as a clearance metric.

Test the boundaries of an episode

Gymnasium returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info). Termination describes task endings such as goal arrival or collision. Truncation describes an external limit such as running out of allowed steps. A learning algorithm may bootstrap value estimates differently in these cases, so folding both into an unexplained done flag can alter what it learns.

Run a short controlled timeout:

python3 - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from arc_rl.nav_core import FastNavEnv, Scenario
scenario = Scenario.boxed_room()
scenario.max_episode_steps = 3
env = FastNavEnv(scenario=scenario, randomise_start=False, lidar_noise_std=0)
env.reset(seed=7)
for k in range(3):
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(np.zeros(2, dtype=np.float32))
    print(k + 1, terminated, truncated, info['termination_reason'])
env.close()
PY

The stationary robot should remain nonterminated, with truncation on step 3. Inspect the goal/collision branches in step() and design one boundary test for each using an explicitly controlled scenario. If two conditions coincide, record both flags and inspect the reported reason rather than assuming they are mutually exclusive.

Then run a weak reference policy on the same geometry seed:

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy random --seeds 500 \
  --out results/lab08_random

Compare paths and termination reasons with the gap baseline. One episode cannot rank policies generally; it can reveal that the loop moves, stops and reports what actually occurred. collision_free_success requires both arrival and zero collisions, so an ambiguous arrival/contact transition is not counted as a clean delivery.

Build a complete small environment before extending the warehouse

Focus on one part of the delivery: the final straight approach along an empty corridor when the robot is already facing its goal. The remaining distance is our observation, and a fraction of maximum forward speed is our action. This smaller problem lets you write every part of an environment yourself. It will be trained separately in Lab 9, before returning to the warehouse task.

Write approach_env.py in your student package. Start with the spaces and reset, then implement the movement equation and ending conditions:

import gymnasium as gym
import numpy as np


class ApproachEnv(gym.Env):
    """A final straight approach to a goal 1 m along an empty corridor.

    This teaching task has one action and one observation. It does not share
    the warehouse policy's 29-input, 2-action interface.
    """
    metadata = {'render_modes': []}

    def __init__(self):
        self.action_space = gym.spaces.Box(0.0, 1.0, (1,), np.float32)
        self.observation_space = gym.spaces.Box(0.0, 1.0, (1,), np.float32)
        self.x = 0.0
        self.steps = 0

    def observation(self):
        return np.array([max(0.0, 1.0 - self.x)], dtype=np.float32)

    def reset(self, *, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self.x = float(self.np_random.uniform(0.0, 0.2))
        self.steps = 0
        return self.observation(), {'x_m': self.x}

    def step(self, action):
        speed = 0.5 * float(np.clip(action[0], 0.0, 1.0))
        previous = self.x
        self.x = min(1.0, self.x + speed * 0.1)
        self.steps += 1
        terminated = self.x >= 0.98
        truncated = self.steps >= 50 and not terminated
        reward = (self.x - previous) - 0.01 + float(terminated)
        return self.observation(), reward, terminated, truncated, {'x_m': self.x}


def main():
    env = ApproachEnv()
    observation, info = env.reset(seed=7)
    for step in range(50):
        observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(np.array([1.0]))
        print(step + 1, observation, reward, terminated, truncated)
        if terminated or truncated:
            break
    env.close()

A Box describes a numeric array’s bounds, shape and dtype. (1,) means an array containing one value. reset calls the base-class reset to initialise Gymnasium’s random generator, then chooses a reproducible starting position between 0 and 0.2 m. The goal stays at x=1 m. options is part of the API; this small environment accepts it but has no optional reset settings.

The motion equation is new position = old position + speed × time. One step lasts 0.1 s; action 1 gives 0.5 m/s, hence 0.05 m per step. Action 0 leaves the robot still. We cap x at 1 m so this task cannot overshoot the goal. Reaching within 0.02 m ends the task; otherwise 50 steps, or 5 simulated seconds, imposes a time limit. This environment gives success priority if both happen together. Other environments may report both flags, as you observed in FastNavEnv.

The reward adds distance progress, subtracts 0.01 per step and adds 1 on success. An ordinary full-speed step earns 0.05-0.01=0.04; standing still earns -0.01. Those numbers specify an objective. The empty corridor has no obstacle sensor, collision model or steering, so success here establishes only this small skill.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/approach_env.py and add 'approach_env = robot_workshop.approach_env:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

Gymnasium and NumPy are Python dependencies supplied by the course VM. For a portable standalone distribution, declare/install them as Python requirements; they are not ROS message packages. Keep using the course Python interpreter so installed ROS and learning dependencies remain compatible.

ros2 run robot_workshop approach_env

The printed sequence should reach termination before the step limit. Replace the demonstrated action with zero and verify timeout instead. Repeat the same seed and check the starting position; change the seed and inspect the change. Write these three checks before editing the reward. They distinguish a working environment from a policy that merely happens to get a good score.

The student package is being used to organise executable Python here; this program launches no ROS node. Your model has one input and one output, whereas FastNavEnv has 29 inputs and two outputs. Keep those model families separate. The larger environment adds heading, range geometry, collision checks and moving obstacles to the same reset/step structure you have now written.

Establish the learning baseline

Keep your actual trajectory, the decoded observation example, the action unit check and the short timeout trace. Identify one interface assumption most likely to fail when replaced with real ROS data. That is a concrete engineering problem for Lab 10, while Lab 9 can now train against a known, inspectable contract.

Optional extension: run Gymnasium’s or Stable-Baselines3’s environment checker on FastNavEnv, then interpret one deliberately introduced shape or dtype error. Passing the checker verifies API consistency, not realistic physics or useful rewards.

  • Gymnasium custom environments: compare the API with your reset/step trace.
  • Gymnasium time-limit handling: why timeout and task termination must remain distinct.
  • Gymnasium: A Standard Interface for Reinforcement Learning Environments (2024 preprint; revised 2025): the research context for a shared environment contract.

Lab 9: Train and evaluate a navigation policy

In Lab 8 you ran a fixed policy through repeated observation-action steps. Today the policy is a neural network whose parameters are updated from those experiences. Training changes that network; evaluation runs the saved network without updating it to measure what it can do.

Two-hour mission: train a small navigation policy, explain how its reward and PPO update connect to behaviour, and evaluate it on layouts excluded from training. Use trajectories and task outcomes to assess the result alongside the reward curve.

Budget 15 minutes for rewards and data splits, 30 for your small training loop, 35 for the warehouse pilot, 25 for evaluation and 15 for interpretation. Training throughput depends on the VM. The core uses a short pilot; longer runs or a second reward can continue outside the session or use instructor-provided checkpoints with matching metadata. Use the shared setup and stop Gazebo.

What does training change?

Our environment defines the task. A learned policy has adjustable numbers, often the weights of a neural network, that determine which actions it chooses. Training changes those numbers using collected experience. Evaluation runs the resulting policy to measure its behaviour under stated conditions.

PPO, short for proximal policy optimisation, is the learning method used here. It collects examples of actions and outcomes, estimates which actions were better than expected, and updates the policy while limiting how strongly some changes are rewarded by its objective. The worked calculation below explains its clipping rule. An improving training reward does not by itself prove good navigation in a new layout; that requires separate evaluation.

Separate practice, validation and final test layouts

Think of layouts as practice rooms and check rooms. A policy that succeeds only in its practice rooms has not yet demonstrated that it can handle another room. We therefore reserve layouts before training. Validation helps choose among changes; a final test is kept unused until those choices are finished.

Lab 8 established a working observation and action contract. Today keep that contract fixed while changing the policy. Use teaching/train_policy.py, which restricts training geometry to a bank of seeds 0-99. Validation uses 500-509; final testing reserves 1000-1009 until your decisions are fixed.

This explicit bank matters. The original general-purpose training script draws from a much larger seed range, so simply choosing seed 500 for evaluation would not prove that its geometry was excluded from training. A seed is an input to the generator, not a label that automatically creates a dataset split.

Inspect training_bank() and FastNavEnv.reset(): unseeded resets draw a fresh integer, and the bank maps it modulo 100 before constructing geometry. Training still experiences fresh stochastic sensor noise. The optimizer seed is another source of randomness; it is not the same thing as a held-out environment split. Different geometry seeds reduce deliberate overlap but do not prove that every generated layout is structurally different.

Calculate the incentive before training on it

Open the reward functions in arc_rl/nav_core.py. For dense progress, the main term is three times the decrease in goal distance, with time, proximity and turning penalties, plus terminal goal/collision bonuses. For a transition from 2.00 m to 1.98 m, angular speed 0.4 rad/s and minimum beam 0.30 m:

python3 - <<'PY'
from arc_rl.nav_core import RewardTerms, reward_dense_progress, reward_sparse_safe
t = RewardTerms(previous_goal_distance=2.0, goal_distance=1.98,
                min_beam=0.30, linear_velocity=0.2, angular_velocity=0.4,
                reached_goal=False, collided=False, step_index=1)
print('dense:', reward_dense_progress(t))
print('sparse:', reward_sparse_safe(t))
PY

Expect dense reward approximately 0.018 and sparse reward approximately -0.08. The dense calculation is 0.06 - 0.01 - 0.03 - 0.002. These are designed incentives, not physical measures of navigation quality. The sparse function also includes ongoing penalties, so “sparse” here means that positive success feedback is sparse, not that every nonterminal reward is zero.

The final goal gives +60 in the dense reward or +100 in the sparse reward; collision gives the corresponding negative bonus. The environment separately adds +30 when advancing an intermediate checkpoint. Read both step() and the reward callable to understand the full return. A reward function inspected in isolation would miss that checkpoint term.

For a fixed goal, moving 0.2 m closer gives +0.6 progress reward, while moving 0.2 m farther gives -0.6. Those terms cancel when added without discounting: repeatedly moving closer and farther does not create unlimited net progress reward. A buggy positive-only progress term could reward such motion. Discounting, terminal bonuses, checkpoint changes and other penalties still affect behaviour. If a policy circles, inspect its transition/reward trace before assigning a generic “reward hacking” explanation.

Follow one PPO collection-and-update cycle

The training algorithm is PPO, Proximal Policy Optimisation. Its basic cycle is: collect attempts with the current policy, estimate which actions worked better than expected, then adjust the policy to favour useful actions. It limits part of the update incentive so the policy is not encouraged to change too abruptly based on one collected batch.

The terms in the training code describe this cycle:

Term Meaning in our experiment
Transition One observation, action, reward and resulting observation
Return Rewards accumulated over future steps, possibly discounted
Value estimate The model’s prediction of future return from a situation
Advantage An estimate of how much better an outcome was than that expectation
Batch / minibatch Collected examples / a smaller group used in one update
Epoch One pass through the collected training examples

Discounting weights rewards further in the future less strongly. For example, a discount factor of 0.99 multiplies a reward one step ahead by 0.99, two steps ahead by 0.99 squared, and so on. This changes the training objective; it does not change the simulated seconds recorded for an episode.

A neural network builds a decision by combining inputs with adjustable numbers called weights. A hidden unit computes a weighted sum plus a bias, then applies a nonlinear function. Layers combine these intermediate features. Learning adjusts weights using the loss gradient, which indicates how small changes would affect the training objective. A learning rate sets the update scale. There is no guarantee that a finite training run finds the best possible rule.

The policy is a small multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers of 64 units. It maps the 29-value observation to a distribution over two actions. During training the algorithm samples actions to explore; during our evaluation predict(..., deterministic=True) selects the model’s deterministic prediction. Deterministic action selection does not remove stochasticity from the environment.

The helper uses four environments in DummyVecEnv. They are stepped sequentially inside one process, providing several episode streams; this is not four parallel worker processes. With n_steps=512, one collection contains 2048 transitions. PPO uses the collected returns/value estimates to estimate advantages, then updates the policy with minibatches of 256 over ten epochs.

The clipped objective limits the incentive for a large change in action probability during an update. It does not impose a hard bound on every network weight or guarantee collision avoidance. The value model estimates future return, the entropy term encourages exploration, and the reward definition determines what return means. Read the constructor arguments in the helper and connect each of these roles to a parameter before tuning it.

Write the training and evaluation loop for your own environment

Train the small approach task you built in Lab 8 first. The purpose is to assemble the learning pipeline yourself: instantiate the environment, wrap its episode reporting, construct PPO, learn, save, reload and evaluate. Afterwards, apply the same sequence to the supplied warehouse environment with its explicit training bank.

Write train_approach.py:

from pathlib import Path
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.monitor import Monitor
from robot_workshop.approach_env import ApproachEnv


def main():
    output = Path('models/student_approach.zip')
    if output.exists():
        raise FileExistsError('Keep the earlier model; choose a new output filename')
    output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    env = Monitor(ApproachEnv())
    try:
        model = PPO('MlpPolicy', env, n_steps=128, batch_size=64,
                    policy_kwargs={'net_arch': [32, 32]}, seed=0,
                    device='cpu', verbose=1)
        model.learn(total_timesteps=2048)
        model.save(str(output))
    finally:
        env.close()
    model = PPO.load(str(output), device='cpu')
    for seed in (100, 101, 102):
        test = ApproachEnv()
        observation, info = test.reset(seed=seed)
        for step in range(50):
            action, _ = model.predict(observation, deterministic=True)
            observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info = test.step(action)
            if terminated or truncated:
                print(seed, 'success:', terminated, 'steps:', step + 1)
                break
        test.close()

Monitor records episode returns and lengths. PPO owns the neural networks and update algorithm; we use this tested implementation while writing the task and experimental loop ourselves. learn updates the model; predict chooses actions without a training update. Reloading checks that the saved artifact is actually usable. An output filename is part of your experimental record, so the script refuses to overwrite it.

Here the environment count is one, n_steps=128, and batch_size=64: each collection contains 128 transitions, divided into two minibatches per epoch. The later warehouse helper uses four environments and different settings; those numbers are not properties of PPO itself. This approach pilot uses 2,048 transitions and is deliberately much smaller than the warehouse run.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/train_approach.py and add 'train_approach = robot_workshop.train_approach:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

Stable-Baselines3 and its PyTorch dependency are supplied by the VM’s AI setup. From the repository root in a terminal with your student overlay sourced:

ros2 run robot_workshop train_approach

The output model is models/student_approach.zip. Record the reported success and step counts for the three evaluation starts. These starts use different seeds but the same small corridor task; this is a pipeline check, not evidence of generalisation to new obstacle layouts. Do not pass this one-input model to teaching.rollout, which requires the warehouse observation/action contract.

Build one comparison yourself: use constant action 1.0 on those same three starts and compare completion steps. A learned model has no reason to beat that obvious rule in this empty corridor. Learning becomes useful when a handwritten rule is difficult to specify or adapt, not because a network must outperform every simple baseline. Keep the pilot, then continue with the warehouse commands below.

Work through one update incentive numerically

A return is a weighted sum of rewards. With rewards 1 now and 2 next step, and discount 0.9, the two-step return is 1 + 0.9*2 = 2.8. If a value estimate predicted 2.0, the simple return-minus-value advantage would be 0.8. PPO normally uses a more detailed multi-step estimate, but the sign has the same purpose: favour actions with better-than-predicted outcomes and discourage worse ones.

For a discrete illustration, suppose an observed action had probability 0.20 under the collection policy and 0.30 after an update. The ratio is 1.5. With a positive advantage of 2 and a clip range of 0.2, the clipped policy objective uses the smaller of 1.5*2=3 and 1.2*2=2.4, namely 2.4. Increasing this ratio further no longer improves that sample’s clipped term. For continuous actions, PPO uses a probability-density ratio rather than the probability of an exact real-valued action. Clipping is an update objective, not a physical speed limit.

Run a measured training pilot

python3 -m teaching.train_policy --reward dense_progress \
  --steps 20480 --seed 0 --name lab09_dense_pilot_s0

The helper prints training statistics and saves models/lab09_dense_pilot_s0.zip plus a JSON metadata file. It refuses an existing model name to preserve previous evidence. Metadata records the geometry bank, optimizer seed, reward, interface constants, requested/actual steps and elapsed time. Because PPO collects complete rollout batches, actual steps can exceed a requested total that is not a multiple of 2048.

In another terminal, view recorded training summaries:

tensorboard --logdir runs --port 6006

Open http://localhost:6006 in the VM browser. Select the pilot’s run and inspect episode return and episode length alongside loss/update indicators. If nothing appears immediately, let a collection/update finish and refresh. A rising return can result from partial progress without successful delivery, so continue to the trajectory evaluation even if the curve looks promising.

Use the pilot’s elapsed time to estimate a larger run. If there is sufficient time, start a new run:

python3 -m teaching.train_policy --reward dense_progress \
  --steps 200000 --seed 0 --name lab09_dense_full_s0

This starts a fresh model, not a continuation of the pilot. If the full run does not fit the class, evaluate the pilot and label its budget honestly. Poor early performance is a usable result when it reveals the difference between a functioning pipeline and a trained solution.

Compare on exactly the same validation episodes

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy gap \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab09_gap_validation

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy ppo \
  --model models/lab09_dense_pilot_s0.zip \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab09_ppo_validation

Use the full model filename instead if you completed it, and record which model you tested. Both commands use the same generator, starts, noise setting and episode rules. The runner resets each episode and writes per-seed paths and metrics. Compare the paired rows by seed; averaging unrelated layouts would hide whether a difficult layout affected both controllers.

Report collision-free successes as a count out of ten, collisions and timeouts. Compare travel time and path length for matched successful cases; a controller that crashes early can have a deceptively short mean path. Inspect at least one failure trajectory and connect it to beam/goal geometry. Do not claim a general advantage from a small sample or one training seed.

The runner’s return_dense is calculated with the same dense reward for all evaluated policies, even when a policy was trained with another reward. It is diagnostic. The main comparison remains physical task outcomes, because rewards can encode different preferences and arbitrary scales.

Choose one change from the results

Choose a change from a measured failure. If the policy moves toward goals but cuts close to obstacles, compare a safety-oriented reward at the same training budget and optimizer seed:

python3 -m teaching.train_policy --reward sparse_safe \
  --steps 20480 --seed 0 --name lab09_sparse_pilot_s0

Evaluate it with the same ten validation seeds and a new output directory. Do not promise that the sparse policy will learn safer behaviour in a short budget; sparse positive feedback may slow learning. If time is limited, finish the diagnosis and specify the controlled experiment instead of presenting an unrun result.

Keep model/metadata pairs, the validation CSVs, a training-curve image and a failure explanation with a proposed repair. Leave seeds 1000-1009 unused until your model and switching decisions are frozen in Lab 10.
