Lab 10: Test hybrid control and build a ROS command gate

You now have two ways to choose motion: a handwritten controller and a learned policy. Hybrid control uses both, with a rule deciding which one supplies the current command. We are not training a new switching network today; we will inspect a small explicit rule and test whether combining the controllers actually helps.

Two-hour mission: combine the classical baseline with your learned policy, measure when control changes hands, and stress the same missions with noise and delay. Finish with a decision supported by data and an explicit contract for a future ROS implementation.

Spend 15 minutes on switching, 25 on matched runs, 20 on a stressor, 40 building and checking the ROS command gate, and 20 on the final comparison. Bring a Lab 9 PPO model with metadata. Use the shared setup; no Gazebo process is needed for the core experiment.

Decide which component is allowed to command motion

A system may contain more than one way to choose movement. A conventional controller might guide the robot through most of a route while a learned policy handles a selected part. Hybrid control means combining such methods under an explicit rule. At each moment, the system still needs a clear decision about which command is allowed through.

A command gate checks a candidate command before forwarding it. A timeout defines how long a command may remain usable without a fresh update. A watchdog monitors that timing rule. Limiting speed and rejecting stale commands address specific faults; they do not prove that a route is clear of obstacles. Today we test each rule separately so we can explain exactly what protection it provides.

Make the authority change explicit

Here handover means switching the source of the next command. Both controllers accept the same observation and produce the same two-number action, so the environment can apply either one. We still need to decide when to switch, how long to stay switched and when to return. Those are the important new decisions in this lab.

Open starters/lab10/hybrid.py. The classical controller runs by default. The switch requests learned control only when recent displacement is small and the front sector is tight. The defaults retain 40 position samples, compare displacement with 0.12 m, and require front range below 0.55 m. At 20 Hz, 40 samples span approximately two seconds; sample endpoints are 39 intervals apart, so avoid treating the window as an exact two-second timer.

Once triggered, the learned controller gets 60 steps, or three seconds of commands. This commitment prevents instant switching back and forth around a threshold. A cap of 12 handovers bounds how often the learned policy can be invoked in one episode; it does not by itself impose a collision-safe envelope on either controller.

Read reset() and the end of __call__(). Position history, remaining handover time and statistics must be fresh for every episode. Otherwise a controller could begin the next mission halfway through the previous mission’s recovery. The supplied teaching.rollout constructs a new hybrid per episode and passes the simulator’s current (x,y) explicitly.

This position input is a privileged measurement in the fast simulation. A live robot would need an estimate from odometry/localisation, with stated frame and timing. The older make_hybrid_policy() convenience wrapper estimates progress from goal-relative observations, which can change when the robot rotates or switches waypoints. Do not treat that proxy as an equivalent world-position measurement.

Test the switch separately from policy quality

Use the supplied figure to trace a controlled stalled/tight input, then inspect the helper code that generated it:

python3 -m teaching.figures --out results/lab10_figures
xdg-open results/lab10_figures/lab10_plot.png

The two dummy policies make it easy to identify who supplied each action. The demonstration should show a delayed trigger while history fills, a committed learned interval, and a return to classical control. A working switch can still make navigation worse if the learned policy is poor. Isolating mechanism from performance prevents blaming the wrong component.

Evaluate three alternatives on matched missions

Use your chosen model filename in place of the example if it differs. Run each policy on the same validation seeds:

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy gap \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab10_gap

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy ppo \
  --model models/lab09_dense_pilot_s0.zip \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab10_ppo

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy hybrid \
  --model models/lab09_dense_pilot_s0.zip \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab10_hybrid

The runner reports handover count and learned fraction as well as collision-free success, collisions, time, path length and outcome. Pair the rows by seed. Inspect a case with a handover and one without it. If no handovers occur, the hybrid is effectively the classical controller on these cases; identical results then do not demonstrate useful learned recovery.

If a handover worsens a mission, compare the before/after path near its likely trigger and replay that seed separately. Examine whether the robot was truly blocked, whether turning was legitimate, and whether the front-range threshold represented the body clearance you intended. Laser range is measured from the sensor location; collision clearance concerns the robot footprint.

Record one evidence-based switch change as an optional extension. Keep the model and evaluation seeds fixed when testing that change. A more complex switch is justified only if it resolves a measured failure without concealing new ones.

Add one controlled mismatch

Robustness means how well behaviour holds up when conditions change. Start with a very concrete change: the controller receives old observations. At four 20 Hz control steps of delay, a reading describes the scene 0.20 seconds ago, while the robot has continued moving. We will change this delay alone so its effect is interpretable.

First test observation delay while leaving noise at its baseline value:

python3 -m teaching.rollout --policy hybrid \
  --model models/lab09_dense_pilot_s0.zip --delay 4 \
  --seeds 500 501 502 503 504 505 506 507 508 509 \
  --out results/lab10_hybrid_delay4

Four steps correspond to 0.20 s. The runner delays the entire policy observation, including ranges, goal and velocity fields; it still passes current simulator position to the hybrid’s progress detector. This is a specific partial-delay experiment, not a full network/estimator simulation. Read the queue in teaching/rollout.py: it fills with the reset observation so startup has defined behaviour rather than uninitialised memory.

Repeat with --policy gap and a new output path if you want to claim that the hybrid handles delay better than the classical baseline. Comparing delayed hybrid with undelayed classical would confound architecture and observation age. At 0.5 m/s, 0.20 s corresponds to 0.10 m of travel before considering braking; relate that distance to obstacle clearance in the failure trajectory.

For a separate noise experiment, keep --delay 0 and use --noise 0.04 for all compared policies. The seed fixes the random sequence generator, while different trajectories change which geometry is sensed. Same seed does not mean identical sensor values at physically different positions.

The training helper’s --domain-randomisation samples lidar noise standard deviation between 0.005 and 0.04 m per episode. It does not randomise friction, wheel radius, mass, latency or motor dynamics. If you train a randomised policy, use a new model name and the same training budget, then evaluate it under the same stressors. Call the result a lidar-noise robustness experiment.

Design the missing ROS boundary concretely

Transfer would mean taking a policy from its training environment to another system, such as Gazebo or a physical robot. Sim-to-real specifically means moving from simulation to the physical robot. Matching array shapes is only one requirement; timing, motion, sensing and failure handling also have to agree.

The repository does not contain a complete RosNavEnv that executes learned policies in Gazebo. The ROS Nav2 evaluation adapter is also incomplete for world reset and policy observation. Therefore these runs measure performance in the fast surrogate, not completed sim-to-Gazebo or sim-to-real transfer.

Use the experience from Labs 1-7 to define a future adapter in a short design record with concrete acceptance evidence:

Boundary Implementation needed Evidence before live policy execution
Scan input Subscribe with compatible QoS; check stamp, frame and validity; downsample consistently A recorded scan decodes to the same 24 intended sectors
Goal/pose Transform a map goal into the base frame at a defined time Known poses produce the expected distance, sine and cosine
Reset Restore world, robot, goal, queues and controller state Repeated seeded resets reproduce the intended initial condition
Action output Apply the asymmetric scale, enforce limits, publish through the verified command path Test actions produce measured wheel/body motion with correct signs
Timing/failure Detect stale observations and stopped policy updates; command a defined stop A deliberately interrupted data stream stops motion within the specified bound
Outcome Measure goal, collision/contact, timeout and interventions independently of reward Recorded failure cases produce the expected episode labels

Choose one row and specify an input example, expected output with units, and a deliberate failure to detect. This is problem solving at an interface boundary; it does not require pretending an absent module can be launched.

Build and test one ROS boundary now

The complete learned-policy adapter remains a project-sized task. You can still implement one useful part today: accept candidate velocity messages, limit their magnitudes, and emit zero if the producer stops sending. This connects the learning discussion back to the ROS nodes you have been building since Lab 1.

Use isolated topics /candidate_cmd and /checked_cmd for the experiment. The output is observed in a terminal and has no connection to the robot wheels. Write command_gate.py:

import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.clock import Clock, ClockType
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist


def limited_command(v, w, age_s, timeout_s=0.3):
    if not all(math.isfinite(value) for value in (v, w, age_s)):
        return 0.0, 0.0
    if age_s < 0 or age_s >= timeout_s:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    return max(-0.125, min(0.5, v)), max(-1.8, min(1.8, w))


class CommandGate(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('command_gate')
        self.clock = Clock(clock_type=ClockType.STEADY_TIME)
        self.received_at = None
        self.request = (0.0, 0.0)
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Twist, 'checked_cmd', 10)
        self.subscription = self.create_subscription(Twist, 'candidate_cmd', self.on_command, 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.05, self.tick, clock=self.clock)

    def on_command(self, message):
        self.request = (message.linear.x, message.angular.z)
        self.received_at = self.clock.now().nanoseconds * 1e-9

    def tick(self):
        now = self.clock.now().nanoseconds * 1e-9
        age = float('inf') if self.received_at is None else now - self.received_at
        v, w = limited_command(*self.request, age)
        message = Twist()
        message.linear.x = v
        message.angular.z = w
        self.publisher.publish(message)


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = CommandGate()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        if rclpy.ok():
            rclpy.shutdown()

The first function is pure logic: valid recent input is clipped to the declared speed bounds; invalid or old input becomes zero. The node stores the newest request and republishes at a requested 20 Hz. Its steady clock measures elapsed time without simulation pauses or wall-clock adjustments. The timer uses that same clock, so pausing /clock does not pause this freshness check. Actual callback timing still depends on the operating system and executor.

This watchdog measures time since receipt of a command. Twist has no header, so it cannot detect a command that was already old before arriving. Nor can it detect a live producer repeatedly sending a command based on an obsolete scan. Those require stamped inputs and an observation-age rule. Limiting velocity also does not account for braking distance, footprint or obstacles. The small component has a deliberately precise scope.

Save ~/student_ws/src/robot_workshop/robot_workshop/command_gate.py and add 'command_gate = robot_workshop.command_gate:main', to the existing console_scripts list in setup.py. Add <exec_depend>geometry_msgs</exec_depend> to package.xml. Use the Lab 1 build cycle: a fresh terminal, source ROS and the course underlay, cd ~/student_ws, then colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select robot_workshop. In each running terminal, source ~/student_ws/install/local_setup.bash after the course setup. Keep the entries and files from earlier labs.

Run the gate in A. In B observe output, and in C publish a request:

ros2 run robot_workshop command_gate
ros2 topic echo /checked_cmd
ros2 topic pub --rate 10 /candidate_cmd geometry_msgs/msg/Twist \
  '{linear: {x: 0.8}, angular: {z: 2.5}}'

The output should limit x to 0.5 m/s and z to 1.8 rad/s. Stop only the publisher in C. After the 0.3 s receipt timeout, a subsequent gate callback should output zero. This is a target behaviour to measure, not a hard real-time guarantee. Record the observed delay. Test a negative request as well: -0.4 m/s should be limited to -0.125 m/s. Use ros2 topic info /checked_cmd --verbose to verify that only the observer subscribes during this isolated test.

Next add your own check to limited_command: make the timeout a function argument and test a value exactly on its boundary. The reference treats age 0.3 s as stale. Explain how an accidentally reversed inequality would either reject all fresh commands or keep stale commands alive.

For a future robot integration, a launch file would explicitly remap the gate output into one verified command chain, and every competing command source would need a defined arbitration rule. A Python gate that stops publishing when its own process dies cannot guarantee stopping by itself; the downstream controller needs an independent command timeout. Keep those requirements in your adapter design. Today you have built and measured one real ROS component instead of leaving the entire boundary as a drawing.

Finish the design, then run the reserved tests

After choosing your policy and switch configuration from validation evidence, run the same comparison using seeds 1000-1009 and new output directories. Keep those final results separate. If you revise the design after seeing them, they have become validation data; reserve another untouched set for a new final test rather than continuing to call them unseen.

Report counts and paired cases: where the hybrid helped, where it failed, how often it used learned control, and how the chosen stressor changed outcomes. Keeping the classical controller is a valid outcome if the results support it. Keep the model metadata, CSV/JSON results, two annotated trajectories and the adapter acceptance example. These records should let another student reproduce the comparison and understand its limits.
